Chapter Four: On the Characteristics of All Dharmas (1).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guṇākara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bodhisattva who is skillful regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
To what extent is a bodhisattva called one who is skillful regarding the characteristics of all phenomena?
"To what extent does the Tathāgata designate one as a bodhisattva who is skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena?
When these words had been spoken,
the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Guṇākara:
“Excellent, Guṇamati!
That you are now able to question the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning!”
You have now raised this question out of a desire to benefit and bring peace and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world— including its devas, humans, and asuras—
and in order that they may attain meaningful profit, peace, and happiness.
"You should listen attentively; I shall explain the characteristics of all phenomena for you.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of characteristics of all phenomena. What are these three?
First, the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);..."
Second is the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*);
third is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena?
This refers to the designation of all phenomena as having a conventional identity and its distinctions, even for the purpose of giving rise to verbal expression.
What is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of all phenomena?

That is to say, all phenomena have the nature of dependent origination: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Namely, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise, and so on, until the gathering of this entire great mass of suffering.
What is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all phenomena?
It is the true thusness (*tathatā*) that is equal in all phenomena.

Regarding this true thusness, it is through the causal conditions of the courageous diligence of the assembly of bodhisattvas, and through the causal conditions of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) and non-erroneous reflection, that they are able to penetrate it.

Through this realization, one gradually cultivates and accumulates [merit and wisdom] until, upon reaching unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one finally realizes full perfection. "Good son!
You should know that the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature are just like the affliction of cataracts in the eyes of a person with blurred vision."
Just as a person with cataracts perceives various manifestations of the cataract—
such as hair, feathers, wheels, bees, flies, or mustard seeds, or else the distinct appearances of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—
one should know that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is likewise.
Just as a person with clear vision is free from the affliction of cataracts in the eye, and this very clarity of vision naturally operates within an undistorted sphere of objects;
so too should the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) be understood.
“Good son! For example, it is like a pure crystal gem: if it comes into contact with a blue dye, it resembles the image of an indranīla, mahānīla, or maṇi jewel;
because sentient beings mistakenly grasp it as being an indranīla, mahānīla, or maṇi jewel, they are thereby deluded.”
If it comes into contact with red dye, it resembles an agate maṇi jewel;
because beings falsely grasp it as an agate maṇi jewel, they are thereby deluded.
If it comes into contact with green dye, it resembles a mārakata mani jewel;
because sentient beings falsely grasp it as a mārakata mani jewel, they are thereby deluded.
If it comes into contact with yellow dye, it resembles a golden image;
because sentient beings falsely grasp it as a genuine golden image, they are deluded.
"In this same way, Guṇākara!..."
Just as there is the appearance of coloring upon that pure crystal,
one should know that the linguistic habitual tendencies of the imagined nature upon the dependent nature are likewise so.
Just as there is the false attachment to sapphire, emerald, amber, musāragalva, gold, and so forth upon that pure crystal,
one should know that the attachment to the imagined nature upon the dependent nature is likewise.
Just as that pure crystal gem is, so too should the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) be understood.

Just as all the appearances of sapphire, emerald, amber, musāragalva, and genuine gold upon that pure crystal are, at all times and for all eternity, without reality and without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), so too, upon the dependent nature, by virtue of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), there is, at all times and for all eternity, no reality and no intrinsic nature.
It should be known that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is likewise. Furthermore, Guṇākara!
Because the association of signs and names serves as a condition, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) can be understood.
Because the grasping at the imagined nature upon the dependent nature serves as the condition, the dependent nature can be known;
because the absence of grasping at the imagined nature upon the dependent nature serves as the condition, the perfected nature can be known.

“Good son! If bodhisattvas can, upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, truly understand the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), they will then be able to truly understand all phenomena that are signless (*animitta*).
If bodhisattvas truly understand the dependent nature, they will then be able to truly understand all phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*).”
If bodhisattvas understand the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) as it truly is, they will be able to understand all phenomena characterized by purity as they truly are. "Good son!

If bodhisattvas can, upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), truly understand the phenomenon of signlessness (*animitta-dharma*), they will be able to eliminate phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*);
if they can eliminate phenomena characterized by affliction, they will be able to realize phenomena characterized by purity (*vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa*).

"In this way, Guṇākara! It is because bodhisattvas, as they truly understand the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*);

and because they truly understand all phenomena that are signless (*animitta*), phenomena characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa*), and phenomena characterized by purification (*vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa*)."

Because they understand phenomena that are signless as they truly are, they eliminate all phenomena characterized by defilement; because they eliminate all phenomena characterized by defilement, they realize all phenomena characterized by purity.
To this extent, one is called a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena;
it is to this extent that the Tathāgata designates one as a bodhisattva skilled in the characteristics of all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one does not understand phenomena that are signless, One cannot sever phenomena characterized by defilement.
Because one does not sever phenomena characterized by defilement, One destroys the realization of phenomena characterized by subtle, pure signs."
Failing to observe the many faults of conditioned phenomena, they are harmed by the fault of negligence;
dwelling in the midst of both stable and unstable states through indolence, they suffer ruin and are truly pitiable.

Chapter Five: The Characteristics of the Lack of Intrinsic Nature (2). The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Chapter Five: The Characteristics of the Lack of Intrinsic Nature. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Once, while staying alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
"The Blessed One has, through countless gateways, spoken thus:

'Regarding all the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the aggregates, their characteristic of arising, their characteristic of cessation, their permanent abandonment, and their full comprehension.'"
As it was said regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), so it is with the sense bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the nutriments (*āhāra*).
Through immeasurable gateways, it has been taught:
"The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the truths are to be fully known (*parijñeya*), abandoned (*prahātavya*), realized (*sākṣātkartavya*), and cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*)."
Through immeasurable gateways, he has previously taught:
"The specific characteristics of all elements (*dhātu*), their various elemental natures, their non-uniform elemental natures, their permanent abandonment, and their thorough knowledge."
Through immeasurable gateways, he has previously taught:

"Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), the things to be countered (*vipakṣa*), and the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): that which has not yet arisen is caused to arise; that which has already arisen is made firm, not forgotten, repeatedly practiced, increased, and expanded."
As it was said regarding the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, so it is likewise here.
Through immeasurable gateways, it has been taught:

"The specific characteristics, the remedies, the things to be remedied, and the cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path—causing that which has not yet arisen to arise, and once arisen, causing it to remain firm, not to be forgotten, to be practiced repeatedly, and to increase, expand, and become vast."
The World-Honored One further said:
"All dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature; they are without arising and without cessation; they are quiescent from the beginning and are by their very nature nirvāṇa."
"I do not yet understand, Blessed One, based on what underlying intention you have made such a statement:
'All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by their very nature in a state of nirvāṇa.'"

I now inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this meaning; I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion, will explain the underlying intent behind the teaching that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Paramārthasamudgata!
"What you have contemplated is most consistent with reason.
Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"

It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning. You have raised this question out of a desire to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, out of compassion for the world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—and for the sake of enabling them to attain meaningful benefit and happiness.

Listen attentively; I shall explain for you the underlying intent behind what has been said: that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by their very nature in a state of nirvāṇa.

“Paramārthasaṃvṛti! You should know that it was based on the three kinds of naturelessness with intentional meaning that I declared all phenomena to be without intrinsic nature—namely, the naturelessness of characteristics, the naturelessness of arising, and the ultimate naturelessness.”
“Good son! What is the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the characteristics of all phenomena?
It refers to the imagined characteristic of all phenomena.”

Why is this? Because these are established as characteristics by way of conventional designation, and not established as characteristics by way of their own intrinsic characteristics; therefore, they are said to have the nature of being without intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
“What is the nature of the lack of self-nature in the arising of all phenomena?
It refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Why is this so?”
This exists by virtue of the power of other-dependent conditions and does not exist inherently; therefore, it is called the "naturelessness of arising.
What is the ultimate naturelessness of all phenomena?
It means that because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature by virtue of their nature of being produced, they are said to have no intrinsic nature;
these very dependently originated phenomena are also called the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.

Why is this? Among all phenomena, that which is an object of pure observation, I demonstrate as the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*); whereas the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) is not an object of pure observation, and for this reason it is also designated as the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all phenomena, which is also called the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*). Why is this?

The dharmic selflessness (*dharmanairātmya*) of all phenomena is termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*), and it is also termed the lack of intrinsic nature; for it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of all phenomena and is that which is revealed by the lack of intrinsic nature.
For these reasons, it is called the ultimate nature of being without self-nature.
"Good son! Just as a flower in the sky, you should know that the nature of being without self-nature in terms of characteristics is likewise."
Just as an illusory image has the nature of being without intrinsic nature in its arising, so too should one understand [the nature of phenomena];
likewise, one should understand that a portion of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature is also thus.
For example, just as space is manifested solely by the lack of intrinsic nature in all forms and pervades all places;
so too should one understand the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature in a portion [of phenomena], for it is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and pervades all things.
“Good son! Based on these three kinds of naturelessness, I have spoken with intentional meaning, saying:
‘All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.’”

"Paramārthasamudgata! You should know that it was based on the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) that I spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), saying:
'All phenomena are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.'"
Why is this? If dharmas lack any self-characteristic whatsoever, then there is no arising;
if there is no arising, then there is no cessation.
If there is neither arising nor ceasing, then it is primordially quiescent;
if it is primordially quiescent, then it is by nature in nirvāṇa.
This is because within this [reality], there is not even the slightest thing that could further be brought to parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, based on the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*),
I have spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that "all phenomena are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa."
“Good son! I also, based on the ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic nature as manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, spoke with intentional meaning, saying:
‘All phenomena are unarisen, unceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa.’”

Why is this? Because the ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic nature, which is manifested by the selflessness of phenomena, is at all times and for all eternity the dharmatā of all phenomena—abiding and unconditioned.

Because it is dissociated from all defilements, and because the *dharmatā* of all phenomena abides at all times and for all eternity, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Being unconditioned, it is without arising and without cessation;
because it is dissociated from all defilements, it is primordially quiescent and by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, based on the ultimate nature of lack of intrinsic existence as manifested by the selflessness of phenomena,
I have spoken with intentional meaning that "all dharmas are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature nirvāṇa."
"Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata!

It is not because sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings perceive the *parikalpita-svabhāva* as their own nature that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness; nor is it because they perceive the *paratantra-svabhāva* and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* as their own nature that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness.
Rather, it is because sentient beings superimpose the *parikalpita-svabhāva* upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* that I establish the three kinds of naturelessness."
"By means of the characteristic of the imagined nature, those sentient beings give rise to verbal expressions with respect to the dependent nature and the perfected nature."

In whatever way discourse arises in accordance with suchness, through the perfuming of the mind by discourse, through the subsequent conceptualization of discourse, and through the latent tendencies of discourse, one clings to the characteristics of the imagined nature within the dependent nature and the perfected nature.

"In whatever way one adheres [to things], in that very same way one adheres to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
By reason of this, the *paratantra-svabhāva* arises in future lives.

Due to these causes and conditions, one becomes defiled either by the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), or by the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), or by the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*). One gallops for a long time and wanders for a long time through saṃsāra without rest, experiencing various sufferings—whether in the hells, among animals, among hungry ghosts, in the heavens, among the asuras, or among human beings."
"Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata!

If there are sentient beings who, from the very beginning, have not planted roots of virtue, have not purified their obscurations, have not matured their mental continuums, have not extensively cultivated resolute conviction, and have been unable to accumulate the two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom.
For their sake, I have taught all phenomena based on the nature of the non-substantiality of arising.
Having heard this, they are able to partially comprehend that among all dependently arisen formations, things are impermanent, unstable, insecure, and subject to transformation and decay.

Once they have developed fear toward all formations and a deep sense of revulsion, they restrain themselves from evil; they are able to refrain from committing unwholesome deeds and diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas.

By virtue of practicing wholesome causes, those who have not yet planted roots of goodness are able to plant them; those whose obscurations have not yet been purified are able to purify them; and those whose mental continuums have not yet matured are able to bring them to maturity.
Due to these causes and conditions, they extensively cultivate resolute conviction and also extensively accumulate the two kinds of provisions: merit and wisdom.

Although they thus plant various roots of goodness and even accumulate the two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom—they are nevertheless unable to understand, as they truly are, the naturelessness of characteristics and the two kinds of ultimate naturelessness within the naturelessness of arising.

Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one has not yet correctly become weary of them, has not yet correctly become dispassionate toward them, has not yet correctly attained liberation, and has not yet fully liberated oneself from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*jāti-saṃkleśa*).

The Tathāgata further taught them the essential points of the Dharma, namely, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

This was for the purpose of enabling them to correctly feel revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), to correctly become dispassionate toward them, and to correctly attain liberation; that they might transcend all defilements of affliction (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), transcend all defilements of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and transcend all defilements of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).

"Having heard this Dharma thus taught, he is able to correctly believe in and understand the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in arising, as well as the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in characteristics and the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the ultimate; he discriminates and contemplates it, penetrating it as it truly is;
and regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), he is able to refrain from clinging to the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."

By means of the wisdom that is not permeated by verbal expression, by means of the wisdom that does not follow after the perception of verbal expression, and by means of the wisdom that is free from the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of verbal expression, one can extinguish the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*);
supported by the power of wisdom within this present life, one can forever sever and extinguish the causes for future lives.

By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to correctly feel weary of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), correctly become free from desire for them, and correctly attain liberation; one is able to achieve universal liberation from the three types of defilements (*saṃkleśa*): those of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth (*jāti*).
"Furthermore, Paramārthasamudgata!
Those sentient beings belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvakayāna also realize unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa by means of this very path and this very track."
Sentient beings of the pratyekabuddha-vehicle lineage and sentient beings of the tathāgata-vehicle lineage also realize unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa by means of this path and this course of practice.
All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas share this single, wondrously pure path; they all equally attain this single ultimate purity, and there is no second.
It is based on this that I have spoken with intentional meaning, saying:
"There is only one vehicle.

This does not mean that within the realm of all sentient beings there are no various types of spiritual lineages, nor the distinctions among sentient beings of dull faculties, middling faculties, or sharp faculties.

“Good son! If a person belonging to the lineage of a śrāvaka who is exclusively inclined toward tranquility, even though they receive the various skillful means of courageous application and guidance established by all the Buddhas, they can ultimately never be made to sit at the site of enlightenment and realize unexcelled, complete, and perfect awakening.”

Why is this? Because they have, from the very beginning, possessed only an inferior spiritual lineage; because their compassion has always been weak; and because they have always been terrified by all forms of suffering.
Because their compassion is consistently weak, they consistently turn their backs on the task of benefiting all sentient beings;
because they consistently fear all forms of suffering, they consistently turn their backs on the undertaking of initiating various conditioned activities.

I never say that one who entirely turns their back on the work of benefiting sentient beings, or who entirely turns their back on the undertaking of initiating all practices, will be able to sit at the site of enlightenment and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; therefore, such a person is called a "śrāvaka who exclusively tends toward tranquility."
If a person belonging to the śrāvaka lineage turns their dedication toward bodhi, I also describe them as a bodhisattva by way of another designation. Why is this?

Because once they have already been liberated from the afflictive obscurations, if they receive the awakening of the Buddhas, their minds may likewise attain liberation from the cognitive obscurations.

Because they initially cultivate preparatory practices for their own benefit in order to be liberated from the afflictive obscurations, the Tathāgata designates them as belonging to the śrāvaka lineage.
"Furthermore, Paramārthasaṃudgata!

Thus, within this well-expounded and well-ordained Dharma-Vinaya of mine, and within these well-taught instructions spoken with a most pure intention, various differences in the mental dispositions of sentient beings can be observed."

"Good son! It is solely based on these three kinds of naturelessness that the Tathāgata, through profound intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), has taught the essential points of all phenomena by means of concealed expressions within the sūtras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) that he proclaimed—namely, that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa."

"In this sutra, if there are sentient beings who have already planted supreme roots of virtue, who have already purified all hindrances, who have already matured their mental continuums, who have already extensively cultivated resolute conviction, and who have already been able to accumulate supreme provisions of merit and wisdom—if they hear such a teaching as this, they will understand my profound and intentional speech according to reality; they will give rise to deep faith and understanding in this Dharma, and through non-erroneous wisdom, they will penetrate the meaning of this teaching as it truly is."
Because they have attained thorough penetration and practiced well according to this, they will swiftly realize the most ultimate consummation;
furthermore, they will develop profound pure faith in me, knowing that I am a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who has attained manifest and perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.

"If there are sentient beings who have already planted superior roots of virtue, have already purified their various obscurations, have already matured their mental continuums, and have already extensively cultivated resolute conviction, yet have not yet accumulated superior provisions of merit and wisdom."

Their nature is upright; they belong to the class of those who are upright. Although they lack the power to discern what should be rejected or adopted, they do not dwell within their own dogmatic views.

If they hear such a teaching as this, although they lack the power to understand my profound and secret discourse as it truly is, they will nonetheless be able to give rise to resolute conviction and pure faith toward this Dharma. They will believe that this sūtra was spoken by the Tathāgata, that it is profound, that its profundity is manifest, that it accords with emptiness, and that it is difficult to see and difficult to realize, beyond the reach of discursive thought, not the domain of discursive thought, but something understood only by those who are subtle, discerning, wise, and intelligent.
Regarding the meaning taught in this sutra, they dwell in self-deprecation and speak thus:

"The bodhi of all Buddhas is most profound, and the dharmatā of all phenomena is also most profound; only the Buddha-Tathāgatas can thoroughly comprehend it, whereas it is not something we are capable of understanding."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma for sentient beings of various inclinations;
the wisdom and vision of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are boundless, whereas our own wisdom and vision are like the water in a cow’s footprint.
"Although one may revere this sutra, proclaim it to others, transcribe and preserve it, read and recite it, disseminate it, and offer it profound worship while memorizing and rehearsing it;
yet, because one has not yet initiated the application of cultivation through its meditative signs, one cannot penetrate the words spoken by me with their profound and secret intent."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, those sentient beings are likewise able to increase their two kinds of provisions—merit and wisdom—and they are also able to bring to maturity those whose mental continuums have not yet matured.

"If there are sentient beings—expounding at length until those who have not yet accumulated the superior provisions of merit and wisdom—who are by nature not upright, nor of an upright class; who, although possessing the power to discern what to adopt and what to reject, nevertheless abide within their own dogmatic adherence to views."
Having heard such a teaching as this, they are unable to understand my profound and intentional discourse as it truly is.

Although they develop faith and understanding toward this Dharma, they adhere to its meaning according to the literal expression, claiming that all phenomena are definitively without intrinsic nature, definitively unarisen and unceasing, definitively quiescent from the beginning, and definitively parinirvāṇa by their very nature.
Due to these causes and conditions, one attains the view of non-existence and the view of signlessness regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Because of attaining this view of non-existence and signlessness, one negates all signs as being signless, thereby repudiating the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all phenomena.

Why is this? Because it is only by virtue of the existence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) can be established.

If one views the dependent nature and the perfected nature as being without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), one is likewise negating the imagined nature; therefore, it is said that such a person negates all three natures.
Although they give rise to the notion of "Dharma" regarding my teaching, they do not give rise to the notion of "meaning" regarding its true meaning.

Because they give rise to the notion of "Dharma" regarding my teaching and because they give rise to the notion of "meaning" regarding what is not the meaning, they maintain that this teaching is indeed the Dharma and maintain that this is indeed the meaning.
Although their merit increases because they give rise to faith and understanding toward the Dharma,
their wisdom declines because they give rise to attachment toward what is not meaningful;
and because their wisdom declines, they fall away from vast and immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who hear from others that what is the Dharma is indeed the Dharma, and what is not the meaning is indeed the meaning; if they follow such views, they will conceive the notion of "Dharma" regarding the Dharma and the notion of "meaning" regarding what is not the meaning, thereby grasping at the Dharma as Dharma and what is not the meaning as meaning.
For this reason, you should know that they are identical to those who have fallen away from wholesome dharmas.

If there are sentient beings who do not follow their views, and suddenly hear from them that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa, they will give rise to fear. Having given rise to fear, they will speak thus:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is what was spoken by Māra."
Having formed this interpretation, they slander and revile this sutra.
Due to these causes and conditions, they incur great ruin and encounter a major karmic obstruction.

For this reason, I say that if one gives rise to the view of signlessness regarding all signs, and proclaims what is not the true meaning to be the meaning, this is a means for giving rise to vast karmic obstacles;
for by that, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to fall, leading them to incur great karmic obstacles.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness, have not yet purified their obscurations, have not yet matured their mental continuums, lack extensive resolute conviction, and have not yet accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom.

Their nature is not upright, nor do they belong to the class of those who are upright; although they possess the power and capacity for discernment regarding what to adopt and what to reject, they always abide within their own dogmatic adherence to views.

If they hear such a teaching, they will be unable to understand according to reality my profound and intentional speech; they will likewise fail to develop faith and understanding in this Dharma, conceiving the notion that this Dharma is not the Dharma, and the notion that its meaning is not the true meaning.
Within this Dharma, they grasp at what is not the Dharma; within this meaning, they grasp at what is not the meaning, proclaiming these words:
"This is not the word of the Buddha; it is what was spoken by Māra."

Having formed this view, they slander and revile this sutra, dismissing it as false; by means of countless methods, they destroy and suppress such a sutra, and toward those who have faith in and understand this sutra, they conceive the notion of them being enemies.

Having previously been obstructed by various karmic hindrances, they are further obstructed by such karmic hindrances due to these causes and conditions; such karmic hindrances are easily established from the outset, and even until the end of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, there will be no time of emergence.

“Good son! Thus, within this well-expounded and well-ordained Dharma and Vinaya of mine, taught with an utterly pure intention, such various differences in the mental understandings of sentient beings can be found.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; Unborn and unceasing, they are quiescent from the beginning.
The self-nature of all phenomena is eternally nirvāṇa."
Who among the wise would claim that there is no hidden intent?
I have already revealed that the characteristics, the arising, and the ultimate lack intrinsic nature;
yet those who do not understand this hidden intent of the Buddha will lose the right path and be unable to proceed.
Those who attain purification by means of the various pure paths do so solely by relying on this one [vehicle] and no second;
therefore, the "One Vehicle" is established therein, not because there is no distinction in the nature of sentient beings.
Among the immeasurable births within the realm of sentient beings, you alone deliver a single body toward nirvana;
yet, through great compassion and valor, you realize parinirvāṇa without abandoning sentient beings—this is most difficult to find!
The subtle, inconceivable, and untainted realm—within it, liberation is equal and without distinction;
all goals are accomplished, free from delusion and suffering, described by two different names: permanence and bliss.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The intentional language of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is truly marvelous!”
How rare! Even subtle and most subtle!
Profound and most profound!
It is difficult to penetrate, most difficult to penetrate!
"As I now understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught:

regarding the basis for the signs of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that function within conceptualization, one provisionally designates it as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), whether by way of its essential characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) or its specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)."

To provisionally designate and establish [phenomena] as the arising of the aggregate of form, the cessation of the aggregate of form, or the permanent abandonment and full knowledge of the aggregate of form—whether by way of essential characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) or specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)—is called the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Based on this, the Blessed One establishes the characteristic of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
If it is the very basis for the characteristics of the imagined nature as they are traversed by conceptual construction, this is called the dependent nature.

Based on this, the Blessed One has established the nature of the non-substantiality of the arising of all phenomena (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), as well as one portion of the ultimate nature of non-substantiality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
As I now understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught:

within these very modes of activity (*ākāra*) which serve as the basis for the imagined character (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) that is the object of conceptual construction, because the imagined character is not established as real, that very nature of non-substantiality—which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the objective referent (*ālambana*) of purification—is called the perfected character (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Based on this, the Blessed One establishes the nature of ultimate lack of intrinsic nature as being one part [of the three natures].
Just as it is with the aggregate of form, so it should be explained in detail for all the other aggregates;
just as it is with the aggregates, so it should be explained in detail for each of the twelve bases.
Regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), each link should be explained in detail;
regarding the four kinds of nutriment (*catvāra āhārāḥ*), each nutriment should be explained in detail;
and regarding the six elements (*ṣaḍ dhātavaḥ*) and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ*), each element should be explained in detail.
"This is how I now understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught:

if, within the objective referents of conceptualization—the basis for the signs of the thoroughly imagined nature—one provisionally establishes them as the truth of suffering or the full comprehension of the truth of suffering, whether by way of their essential characteristics or their specific characteristics, these are called the signs of the thoroughly imagined nature."
Based on this, the Blessed One established the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.

If one takes that very basis for the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the object of conceptual construction, as the mode of activity, it is called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Based on this, the Blessed One has established the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature in the arising of all phenomena (*parikalpita-svabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*), as well as a portion of the ultimate nature of the lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
As I now understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught:

within these very modes of activity (*ākāra*) that serve as the basis for the imagined character (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) traversed by conceptual construction, because the imagined character is not established as real, that very nature of the lack of intrinsic nature—the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) which is the object of purification—is called the perfected character (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Based on this, the Blessed One establishes one portion of the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Just as it is with the Truth of Suffering, so it should be explained in detail for the remaining Truths.

Just as it is with the Noble Truths, so it should be explained in detail for each of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and factors of the path.
“Thus, as I now understand the meaning spoken by the Blessed One:

if, within the objective aspects that serve as the basis for the imagined nature—which is the domain of conceptual discrimination—one provisionally establishes a designation as ‘right concentration,’ as well as what is to be remedied and its remedy for that right concentration; and if, when right cultivation has not yet arisen, one causes it to arise, and once it has arisen, one makes it firm, stable, and non-forgetful, cultivating it further so that it increases and expands—whether in terms of essential characteristics or specific characteristics—this is called the imagined nature.”
Based on this, the Blessed One established the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

If it is the very basis for the imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) that are the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is called the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).

Based on this, the Blessed One has established the nature of the non-substantiality of the arising of all phenomena (*parikalpita-svabhāva-niḥsvabhāvatā*), as well as one portion of the ultimate nature of non-substantiality (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
As I now understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught:

within these very modes of activity (*ākāra*) that serve as the basis for the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) traversed by conceptualization, because the imagined characteristic is not established as real, that very nature of non-substantiality—which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and the object of purification—is called the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Based on this, the Blessed One designates one portion of all phenomena as the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature. "Blessed One!
It is like the viśvabheshaja medicine, which should be included in all medicinal powders and elixirs."
"So it is, Blessed One!

Based on these teachings that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa—this definitive teaching on the absence of intrinsic nature—all indeterminate sūtras should be fully integrated and established therein."
“World-Honored One!
Just as a ground for painting is of a single flavor throughout all painting activities—whether blue, yellow, red, or white—and yet is able to manifest those painting activities;”
"So it is, World-Honored One!

Based on these teachings that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature—extending at length until reaching 'nirvana by intrinsic nature'—this definitive teaching on the absence of intrinsic nature is of a single flavor throughout all the non-definitive sūtras; furthermore, it is able to reveal the meanings not yet fully expressed within those various sūtras."
“World-Honored One!
It is as if, when all manner of matured delicacies, cakes, and fruits are infused with refined butter, they produce an even more excellent flavor.
In this same way, World-Honored One!”

Relying on this, they understand that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, and so forth, up to the point that they are by nature in nirvāṇa; thus, regarding the definitive teachings on the absence of intrinsic nature, they set aside all non-definitive sūtras and give rise to supreme joy.
“World-Honored One!
Just as space pervades all places, is of a single uniform taste, and does not obstruct any activities that are undertaken;
so it is, World-Honored One!”

Based on this, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; as explained at length up to the point that they are by nature in nirvāṇa—this definitive teaching on the absence of intrinsic nature is of a single flavor throughout all sūtras of provisional meaning, and it does not obstruct any of the activities practiced by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those of the Mahāyāna.
When these words had been spoken,
the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata,
saying: “Excellent, excellent!
"Good son! You are now able to skillfully understand the profound and intentional meaning of what the Tathāgata has spoken;
furthermore, you have skillfully employed analogies for this meaning, namely: the *viśvabheṣaja* medicine of the world, variegated colors on the ground, clarified butter, and space."
Paramārthasamudgata!
It is so, it is so! There is no other way.
"So it is, so it is! You should receive and uphold this.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

At one time, in Vārāṇasī, at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana, you turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma for those who had set out on the vehicle of the śrāvakas, by means of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.”
Although this is most marvelous and exceedingly rare, among all the gods and humans of the world, none previously had been able to turn it in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was surpassable and subject to further refinement; it was of provisional meaning and served as a basis for various disputes.
“World-Honored One!

In the past, during the second period, you turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the hidden mode of teaching, solely for those who had set out to practice the Mahāyāna, based on the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are unarisen, unceasing, primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.”

Although it was even more marvelous and exceedingly rare, the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was still surpassable, subject to further interpretation, not yet of definitive meaning, and served as a basis for various disputes.
“World-Honored One!

In this present third period, for the sake of those who have set out upon all vehicles, you have turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the characteristics of clear manifestation, based on the fact that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, unarisen, unceasing, originally quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa—namely, the nature of being without intrinsic nature.”
This is the foremost marvel and the most rare occurrence.
The wheel of Dharma now turned by the Blessed One is unsurpassed and allows no room for contradiction; it is the definitive meaning, not a basis for various disputes.

“Bhagavān! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having heard this profound teaching of definitive meaning spoken by the Tathāgata—concerning how all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising, without cessation, are primordially quiescent, and are by nature in nirvāṇa—should believe and understand it, write it down, preserve it, honor it, propagate it, receive and recite it, practice it, and reflect upon it according to the truth; and should further initiate application through the signs of such practice, how much merit would they generate?”
When these words had been spoken,
the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata,
saying: “Paramārthasamudgata!
The merit produced by such good sons or good daughters is immeasurable, incalculable, and difficult to illustrate through analogy; I shall now briefly explain a small portion of it for you.

Just as the soil on a fingernail compared to the soil of the great earth does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part; it does not even bear comparison by calculation, reckoning, analogy, or even the *upaniṣad* fraction.

Or, for example, if one were to compare the water in a cow's footprint to the waters of the four great oceans, it would not equal even one hundredth part; to speak extensively, it would not even equal one *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.

In this way, compared to the merit obtained from hearing, believing, and understanding the various sūtras of provisional meaning—even extending to the merit gathered by initiating application through the signs of cultivation—that merit is not even a hundredth part of the merit accumulated from hearing, believing, and understanding these explained sūtras of definitive meaning; it does not even reach a fraction of it, up to and including an *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part.
When these words had been spoken,
the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In this *Saṃdhinirmocana* Dharma-gate, by what name should this teaching be known?
How should I uphold it? The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata, saying:
“Good son! This is called the teaching of the ultimate definitive meaning;

When this teaching of the ultimate definitive meaning was spoken, within that great assembly, six hundred thousand sentient beings gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
