At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Upon what does a bodhisattva rely and in what do they abide when practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā within the Mahāyāna?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

“Good son! You should know that the provisional designation of the bodhisattva-dharmas, together with the non-abandonment of the vow for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, serves as the basis and support for cultivating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* within the Mahāyāna.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has spoken of four kinds of objective referents:
first, the objective referent of the conceptualized image;"
Second, the objective referent that is the non-conceptual image;
third, the objective referent that is the limit of phenomena;
and fourth, the objective referent that is the accomplishment of what was to be done.
Among these four, how many are the objects of śamatha? How many are the objects of vipaśyanā?
And how many are the objects of both?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Good son! One is the objective referent of śamatha, namely, the non-conceptual image;..."
First is the object of observation for vipaśyanā, namely, the conceptual image;
second is the object of observation common to both [śamatha and vipaśyanā], namely, the limit of phenomena and the fulfillment of what is to be done.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, by relying on these four kinds of objects of focus for śamatha and vipaśyanā, succeed in seeking śamatha and becoming skilled in vipaśyanā?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: “Good son!

Just as I have provisionally established the teachings for the sake of all bodhisattvas—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas.”

When a bodhisattva has well heard, well received, well mastered through speech, well investigated with the mind, and well penetrated through vision these teachings, he then dwells alone in a secluded place and attends to them with mental attention according to how they were well reflected upon.
Furthermore, one directs the attention toward this very mind capable of reflection, maintaining it within the internal continuum of the mind.
Because one thus dwells frequently in such correct practice, there arises physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) and mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*); this is called *śamatha*.
In this way, the bodhisattva is able to seek śamatha.

Because he relies upon the attainment of physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi), he observes and resolves upon the internal images that are the objects of samādhi regarding those phenomena as they have been well-considered, thereby relinquishing the characteristics of the mind.

Regarding the objects of knowledge within the images of such a samādhi, that which is able to correctly discern and most thoroughly discern them, and which involves pervasive investigation and pervasive analysis—whether it be receptivity, interest, wisdom, vision, or contemplation—is called vipaśyanā.
"In this way, a bodhisattva is able to skillfully practice vipaśyanā.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
If bodhisattvas take the mind as their object and internally contemplate the mind, what should all those acts of attention be called prior to attaining physical and mental pliancy?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Good son! This is not the mental engagement of śamatha itself; rather, it is the mental engagement associated with the resolute conviction that accords with śamatha."
“World-Honored One!

If bodhisattvas, until they have attained physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), attend to and contemplate the images that serve as objects within internal samādhi—images corresponding to all those dharmas as they have been reflected upon—what should such mental attention be called?”
“Noble son, it is not the mental engagement of vipaśyanā; rather, it is the mental engagement associated with the resolute conviction that accords with vipaśyanā.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Should it be said that the path of śamatha and the path of vipaśyanā are different,
or should it be said that they are not different?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Good son, you should say that it is neither different nor non-different."
Why is it not different?
Because the mind takes as its object the very object of observation of vipaśyanā.
Why is it not non-different?
"Because the conceptualized image is not the object of cognition.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding the images that are the objects of the various *vipaśyanā* samādhis, should one say they are different from this mind,
or should one say they are not different?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
“Good son! You should say there is no difference. Why is that?
Because those images are nothing but consciousness, noble son,
I say that the objects of consciousness are merely manifestations of consciousness.
“World-Honored One!
If that image which is the object of practice is not different from this mind, how can this mind see this very mind?”
“Good son! Within this, there is not even the slightest dharma that can see another slight dharma;
rather, when this very mind arises in such a way, an image corresponding to it appears.”

Good son! Just as when one relies on the surface of a well-polished, pure mirror, taking the physical object as a condition, one sees the original object itself and yet says, "I am now seeing a reflection," and further claims that there is a manifested reflection appearing separately from the object.
"In this way, when this mind arises, a similar yet distinct image that is the object of samādhi appears.
"World-Honored One,
if sentient beings abide in their own nature, is the image that is the object of the mind as it takes form and so forth as its condition also not different from this mind?"
“Good son! There is indeed no difference.
However, due to their inverted cognition, foolish commoners are unable to know images as they truly are—namely, that they are merely consciousness—and thus they form inverted understandings.”
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
to what extent may it be said that a bodhisattva practices vipaśyanā exclusively?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Good son! If one continuously applies attention, one contemplates only the characteristics of the mind."
“World-Honored One!
To what extent may it be said that a bodhisattva practices śamatha exclusively? “Good son!”
"If one applies attention continuously, thinking only of the immediately preceding mind, [is this so]?
"World-Honored One!
To what extent may it be said that a bodhisattva’s śamatha and vipaśyanā proceed in unison and in combination?"
“Noble son! If one correctly contemplates one-pointedness of mind.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the characteristic of the mind? "Noble son,
it refers to the conceptual image that is the object of samādhi and the focal point of vipaśyanā."
“World-Honored One!
What is the uninterrupted mind? “Good son!
"It refers to the mind that takes that image as its object;
this is the object of śamatha. "World-Honored One, what is one-pointedness of mind?"
“Good son! It means to penetrate that the images traversed by samādhi are nothing but consciousness;
or, having penetrated this, to further contemplate their suchness.”
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of vipaśyanā are there?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son,
there are briefly three kinds:"
First, vipaśyanā with signs; second, vipaśyanā through seeking;
third, vipaśyanā through investigation.
What is vipaśyanā with signs? It is the vipaśyanā that consists solely in the conceptualized image which is the object of samādhi.
What is vipaśyanā of investigation?
That is to say, by means of wisdom, one directs the mind toward vipaśyanā in order to thoroughly understand all those various phenomena that have not yet been well understood.
What is the *vipaśyanā* of investigation?

It refers to the mental attention directed toward *vipaśyanā* by means of wisdom, throughout all those various phenomena that have already been thoroughly understood, for the sake of skillfully realizing ultimate liberation.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of śamatha are there?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son!
Because it follows that immediate mind, you should know that within this there are likewise three kinds."
Furthermore, there are eight kinds, because there is one kind of śamatha for each of the stages from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, there are four kinds, because there is one kind of śamatha for each of the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
you have spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the Dharma, and you have also spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā not based on the Dharma.”
What is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the Dharma?
And what is called śamatha and vipaśyanā not based on the Dharma?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

"Good son! If bodhisattvas, in accordance with the characteristics of the dharmas as previously received and contemplated, attain śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding their meaning, this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the dharma."

If bodhisattvas, without depending on the characteristics of the teachings they have received or contemplated, but relying solely on the instructions and exhortations of others, attain śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding their meaning—namely, contemplating the livid-blue, the putrefaction by pus and so forth; or that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; or that all conditioned phenomena are suffering; or that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self; or that nirvāṇa is ultimate tranquility.
Śamatha and vipaśyanā of such types as these are called śamatha and vipaśyanā that do not rely on the Dharma.
Because one attains śamatha and vipaśyanā by relying on the Dharma, I designate the bodhisattva who practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin) as being of sharp faculties;
because one attains śamatha and vipaśyanā without relying on the Dharma, I designate the bodhisattva who practices in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin) as being of dull faculties.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You have spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā that take individual phenomena as their object, and you have also spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā that take composite phenomena as their object.”
What are called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take individual phenomena as their object?
And what are called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take composite phenomena as their object?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son!

If bodhisattvas take individual sūtras and other such teachings as their object, and cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding those teachings as they have been received and reflected upon, this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take individual dharmas as their object."

If a bodhisattva takes all dharmas, such as the various sūtras and so forth, and brings them together into a single mass, a single heap, a single portion, or a single collection, and then attends to them with mental attention, thinking:
"All these dharmas accord with suchness, tend toward suchness, and lead into suchness;
they accord with enlightenment, accord with nirvāṇa, and accord with the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), as well as tending toward it and leading into it."
All these phenomena proclaim immeasurable and innumerable wholesome dharmas.
To cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā by reflecting in this manner is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the totality of phenomena as their object.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

You have spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the small aggregate of dharmas as their object; you have further spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the great aggregate of dharmas as their object; and you have also spoken of śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the immeasurable aggregate of dharmas as their object.”
What is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the small collection of dharmas as their object?
What is called śamatha and vipaśyanā that take the great collection of dharmas as their object?
“What, furthermore, is meant by ‘śamatha and vipaśyanā that take as their object the immeasurable total dharma’?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya: “Good son!”

If one takes as objects various sūtras, up to various treatises on the meaning, and attends to them by way of unifying them into a single mass, it should be known that this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā based on small-scale composite dharmas.

If one attends to and contemplates the dharmas—ranging from the discourses (sūtras) to those that have been received and reflected upon—as a single mass and so forth, rather than as distinct entities, it should be known that this is called śamatha and vipaśyanā taking great, comprehensive dharmas as their object.

If one takes as an object the immeasurable Dharma teachings of the Tathāgatas, the immeasurable phrases and syllables of the Dharma, and the immeasurable successive insights by which they are illuminated—contemplating them as a single mass and so forth, rather than taking as objects everything from what has been received to what has been reflected upon—one should know that this is called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that take immeasurable composite dharmas as their object.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
to what extent is a bodhisattva said to have attained śamatha and vipaśyanā regarding the universal dharmas as objects?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"Good son! One should know that attainment is achieved by virtue of five conditions:
First, at the time of contemplation, one moment by moment dissolves all bases of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*);
second, being free from various conceptualizations, one attains the joy of the Dharma;
third, one understands the immeasurable light of the Dharma, which is characterized by non-differentiation throughout the ten directions.
Fourth, the aspect of non-conceptualization corresponding to the fulfillment of what is to be accomplished—the pure portion—constantly manifests before one;
fifth, for the sake of bringing the dharma-body to full completion, one gathers the increasingly superior and sublime causes of successive stages.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this śamatha and vipaśyanā based on the general dharma, from what point should it be known as ‘penetration’?”
"From what is it named 'attainment'?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Good son!"
From the first stage, the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), it is called "thorough penetration";
from the third stage, the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), it is called "attainment.
O son of good family!

"Bodhisattvas at the stage of initial practice should also train in this by following these mental orientations (*manasikāra*); although they may not yet be praiseworthy, they must not become lax or negligent.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding these śamatha and vipaśyanā, what is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra?
And what is called the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra?
"What is called the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Good son!"

Regarding the characteristics of the phenomena that are sought and examined as they are apprehended, if there is a coarse and manifest experiencing and observation, these various forms of śamatha and vipaśyanā are called the samādhi with directed thought and sustained examination.

If, regarding that sign, although there is no coarse or manifest reception and observation, there is a subtle reception and observation of the mindfulness of that light, such śamatha and vipaśyanā are called the samādhi of "without vitarka and with only vicāra."

If, with respect to those very characteristics of all phenomena, one entirely lacks mental engagement (*manasikāra*), reception, and observation, then these forms of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are called the concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*).
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If there is seeking through śamatha and vipaśyanā, this is called the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra."
If there is śamatha and vipaśyanā involving investigation (vicāra), this is called the samādhi with no vitarka and only vicāra.
If there is śamatha and vipaśyanā taking the total dharma as their object, this is called the samādhi with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the characteristic of cessation?”
"What are the characteristics of exertion?
What are the characteristics of relinquishment?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:

“Good son! When the mind is agitated or when there is fear of agitation, the mental attention toward phenomena that inspire revulsion and the mental attention toward the immediate state of the mind—this is called the sign of tranquility (śamatha-nimitta).”

When the mind has sunk or when there is fear that it might sink, the mental attention to objects that are inspiring and the mental attention to the characteristics of that mind are called the sign of uplifting (*pragraha-nimitta*).

When one is defiled by the two secondary afflictions while on the path of exclusively calming (*śamatha*), the path of exclusively insight (*vipaśyanā*), or the path of their combined practice (*yuganaddha*), the mental attention that is effortless and all mental attention occurring within the spontaneous flow of the mind are called the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*).
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those bodhisattvas who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā know the phenomena and know their meanings.”
"How does one know the Dharma?
How does one know its meaning?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
“Good son! Those bodhisattvas understand phenomena through five aspects:
first, they know names;”
Second, knowledge of phrases;
third, knowledge of syllables;
fourth, knowledge of distinctions.
Fifth is the knowledge of the general.
What is meant by "name"?
It refers to the conventional designation established as a conceptualization of intrinsic nature within all phenomena, both defiled and pure.
What is a phrase (*pada*)?
It refers to that which, within the aforementioned collection of names, is able to proclaim the meanings of both defilement and purification, serving as their support and foundation.
What is a syllable (*vyañjana*)?
This refers to the syllables that serve as the basis for those two.
How does one discern each of them individually?
It is by means of mental attention directed toward their respective objects.
How does one comprehend them through synthesis?
It is by means of attention directed toward a synthesized object.
When all these are thus condensed into one, it is called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*).
This is called the bodhisattva’s knowledge of phenomena.
"Good son! Those bodhisattvas understand meaning through ten aspects:
First, knowing the nature of all that exists;
second, knowing the nature of things as they are;
third, knowing the object of the grasper.
Fourth, knowing the meaning of that which is apprehended;
fifth, knowing the meaning of establishment;
sixth, knowing the meaning of enjoyment.
Seventh, knowing the meaning of inversion;
eighth, knowing the meaning of non-inversion;
ninth, knowing the meaning of affliction;
Tenth is the knowledge of the meaning of purity. "Good son!

As for the nature of the full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), it refers to all the various categories and limits within all defiled and pure phenomena; this is called the nature of the full extent herein."
It is as with the fivefold enumeration of the aggregates (*skandha*), the sixfold enumeration of the internal bases (*āyatana*), and the sixfold enumeration of the external bases;

it is thus for all such cases. "The nature of things as they are" refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) that exists within all phenomena, both defiled and pure; this is what is meant here by "the nature of things as they are."
This further consists of seven types:
first, the *tathatā* of transmigration, which refers to the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) being without priority or posteriority;
second, the *tathatā* of characteristics, which refers to the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) in all dharmas.
Third is the suchness of discernment, which means that all conditioned phenomena are of the nature of consciousness alone;
fourth is the suchness of establishment, which refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering as taught by me;
fifth is the suchness of erroneous practice, which refers to the Noble Truth of Origination as taught by me.
Sixth is the suchness of purity, which refers to the noble truth of cessation that I have taught;
seventh is the suchness of correct practice, which refers to the noble truth of the path that I have taught.

It should be understood that herein, by virtue of the suchness of流转 (pravṛtti-tathatā), the suchness of 安立 (vyavasthāna-tathatā), and the suchness of 邪行 (mithyāpratipatti-tathatā), all sentient beings are equal and identical.
By virtue of the suchness of characteristics and the suchness of discernment, all phenomena are equal and identical.

By virtue of the suchness of purity, the enlightenment of all śrāvakas, the enlightenment of pratyekabuddhas, and unexcelled perfect complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) are equal and identical.
By virtue of the suchness of correct practice, the wisdom embraced by śamatha and vipaśyanā—which take as their object the totality of phenomena through hearing the true Dharma—is perfectly equal.
"The sense of the grasper refers to the five internal bases of form, as well as the mind, mentation, consciousness, and all mental factors.
The sense of the grasped refers to the six external bases."
Furthermore, there is the sense of the grasper and the sense of the grasped.
"The sense of establishment" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), within which all realms of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) can be established.
That is to say: a single village, or a hundred villages, or a thousand villages, or a hundred thousand villages;
or a great earth extending to the ocean's edge, whether it be a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand [times that].
Or one Jambudvīpa, these hundreds, these thousands, or these hundreds of thousands;
or one Caturmahādvīpa, these hundreds, these thousands, or these hundreds of thousands.
Or a single small chiliocosm, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand of these;
or a single medium chiliocosm, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand of these.
Or a single trichiliocosm; or these hundreds, these thousands, or these hundreds of thousands;
or these koṭis, these hundreds of koṭis, these thousands of koṭis, or these hundreds of thousands of koṭis.

Or these are countless, these are hundreds of countless, these are thousands of countless, these are hundreds of thousands of countless; or they are as numerous as the atoms in hundreds of thousands of three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems, throughout the immeasurable and countless world-systems of the ten directions.
"The meaning of enjoyment refers to the fact that, for the sake of enjoyment, the various classes of sentient beings whom I have described appropriate the necessary requisites.

The meaning of perversion refers to the fact that regarding those very objects such as the subject-apprehender (*grāhaka*), one conceives the impermanent to be permanent; this constitutes a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*)."
To conceive of suffering as pleasure, the impure as pure, and non-self as self constitutes a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
The meaning of "non-perversion" is the opposite of these.
One should understand its characteristics as that which can counteract them.
Regarding the meaning of "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*), it refers to the three kinds of defilements within the triple world: first, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*);
[the second, the defilement of karma; and the third, the defilement of birth].
Second is the defilement of karma;
third is the defilement of birth.
"The meaning of purification" refers to those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) that constitute the dissociation from these three types of defilement.
“Good son! You should know that these ten kinds [of meanings] universally encompass all meanings. Furthermore, good son!”
Those bodhisattvas are said to "know the meaning" because they are able to comprehend five kinds of meanings.
What are these five meanings?
First, the thorough knowledge of phenomena (*vastu*).
Second, the full knowledge of the object;
third, the cause of full knowledge;
fourth, the attainment of the fruit of full knowledge.
Fifth, one awakens to this.
"Good son! In this context, that which is to be fully known should be understood as all that is knowable."
That is to say, it refers to either the aggregates, the internal sense bases, or the external sense bases;
all such things as these.
"The meaning of thorough knowledge" refers to the entire range of objects to be known, including all their various categories and distinctions.

That is to say: by way of the conventional or the ultimate; by way of qualities or faults; by way of conditions or time; by way of the characteristics of arising, abiding, or ceasing; by way of being like a disease and so forth; by way of suffering, its origin, and so forth; by way of suchness, the reality-limit, the dharma-realm, and so forth; by way of being extensive or concise; by way of categorical explanation, analytical explanation, explanatory questioning, or setting aside;
or by way of being implicit or explicit: all such categories should be understood as having the meaning of "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

Regarding the "cause of full comprehension," it should be understood as that which can grasp the first two categories of factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), namely the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) or the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Regarding the "fruit of full comprehension," this refers to the discipline (*vinaya*) consisting in the permanent abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) consisting in the total and permanent abandonment of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Furthermore, regarding all the mundane and supramundane qualities—whether shared or unshared—of the śrāvakas and the Tathāgatas that I have taught, one realizes them therein.
"To be awakened to this" means that, within these very dharmas realized, one extensively speaks of, proclaims, and reveals the various liberating knowledges to others.
“Good son! You should know that these five meanings universally encompass all meanings.
Furthermore, good son!”
Because those bodhisattvas are able to comprehend four kinds of meanings, they are said to "know the meaning.
What are these four meanings?
First, the meaning of the mind’s appropriation (*upādāna*).
Second is the sense of experiencing;
third is the sense of discerning;
fourth is the sense of affliction and purification.
"Good son! You should know that these four meanings universally encompass all meanings.
Furthermore, good son!"
Those bodhisattvas are said to "know the meaning" because they are able to comprehend three kinds of meanings.
What are these three meanings?
First, the meaning of the phrasing; [and so forth].
Second is the meaning of meaning;
third is the meaning of the realm. "Good son!..."
Regarding "words, letters, and meanings," these refer to the collections of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.
It should be understood that there are ten kinds of "meanings of meaning":
first, the characteristic of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*); [and so on].
Second, the characteristic of thorough knowledge;
third, the characteristic of perpetual abandonment;
fourth, the characteristic of realization.
Fifth, the characteristic of cultivation;
sixth, the characteristic of the differentiation of categories such as the reality of that very [cultivation];
seventh, the characteristic of the relationship between the basis and that which depends upon it.
Eighth, the characteristics of the factors that obstruct thorough knowledge and so forth;
ninth, the characteristics of the factors conducive to them;
tenth, the characteristics of the faults of not thoroughly knowing and so forth, as well as the merits of thorough knowledge and so forth.
"As for the meaning of 'realm' (dhātu), it refers to five kinds of realms:
first, the vessel world;
second, the realm of sentient beings;"
Third, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
fourth, the realm of those to be disciplined (vineyadhātu);
fifth, the realm of the means for disciplining (vinayopāyadhātu).
“Good son! You should know that these five meanings universally encompass all meanings.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the wisdom consisting of hearing understands its meaning, if the wisdom consisting of reflection understands its meaning, and if the wisdom consisting of cultivation through śamatha and vipaśyanā understands its meaning—what is the distinction between these?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:

"Good son! The wisdom derived from hearing relies upon the literal text; it merely follows what is said, yet has not yet grasped the underlying intention, has not yet been manifested before one, does not fully accord with liberation, and is not yet capable of receiving the meaning that constitutes liberation."

The wisdom arisen from reflection also relies upon the literal text; however, it is not merely according to the letter, for it can skillfully comprehend the underlying intent. Though it has not yet become manifest, it turns toward and accords with liberation, yet it is not yet capable of fully realizing the meaning that constitutes liberation.

If bodhisattvas cultivate the wisdom born of meditation, they rely both on the literal expression and do not rely on the literal expression; they accord with the words yet do not accord with the words, being able to understand the intended meaning. When the image that is the object of samādhi—which corresponds to the objects of knowledge—manifests before them, it is highly conducive to liberation, and they are already able to experience and realize the state of liberation.
“Good son! These are called the three distinctions in the knowledge of meaning.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding those bodhisattvas who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā, knowing the phenomena and knowing their meanings—what constitutes wisdom?
What constitutes vision?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: “Good son!
I have expounded the two distinctions between knowledge and vision through immeasurable gateways; I shall now briefly explain their characteristics for you.”
The sublime wisdom that arises from cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking general phenomena as their object is called "knowledge" (jñāna);
the sublime wisdom that arises from cultivating śamatha and vipaśyanā by taking specific phenomena as their object is called "view" (dṛṣṭi).
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by means of what do the bodhisattvas who cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā apply their attention, and what is it that they attend to?”
"How does one eliminate all signs?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son!"
By means of mental attention to suchness (*tathatā-manasikāra*), one eliminates the signs of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) and the signs of their referents (*artha-nimitta*);
when neither the name nor the intrinsic nature of the name is apprehended, one likewise does not observe the signs upon which they depend—in this way, they are eliminated.
As it is with names, so it should be understood for phrases, syllables, and all meanings.

Even when one does not apprehend the elements (*dhātu*) or the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the elements, one likewise does not observe the characteristics of their basis; in this way, they are eliminated.
“World-Honored One!
Regarding all that is known as the characteristic of the meaning of *tathatā*, can this characteristic of *tathatā* also be eliminated? “Good son!”
Within the meaning of suchness as it is thoroughly understood, there are no signs whatsoever, nor is anything to be apprehended; what, then, could possibly be discarded?
Son of good family!
I say that when one thoroughly understands the meaning of suchness, one can subdue the signs of all phenomena and their meanings; this realization cannot be subdued by anything else.
“World-Honored One!

As the World-Honored One has said, it is like the analogy of a vessel of turbid water, the analogy of an unclean mirror, and the analogy of a stirred spring or pond; one is unable to observe the reflection of one’s own facial features.
If one were capable of doing so, it would be contrary to the aforementioned analogies.”
Thus, if the mind is not well-cultivated, one is incapable of examining suchness as it truly is;
if the mind is well-cultivated, one is capable of such examination.
"What kind of mind capable of observation is being described here?
Based upon which suchness is this statement made?
"O son of good family!

This explains the three types of minds capable of investigation: namely, the mind capable of investigation consisting of hearing, the mind capable of investigation consisting of reflection, and the mind capable of investigation consisting of cultivation.
"This was stated based on the *tathatā* of discernment.
"World-Honored One,

for a bodhisattva who thus understands the meaning of the Dharma and diligently practices the preparatory application (*prayoga*) in order to eliminate all signs (*nimitta*), how many kinds of signs are difficult to eliminate?"
"Who is able to dispel it?
"Good son! There are ten kinds of signs that emptiness can dispel."
What are the ten? First, because one understands the meaning of phenomena (*dharma*), there appear various signs of words and letters;
these can be correctly eliminated by means of the emptiness of all phenomena.
Second, because one understands the meaning of the established *tathatā*, there is the characteristic of a continuous succession of the nature of arising, ceasing, abiding, and changing;
this can be correctly eliminated through the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the absence of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāpara-śūnyatā*).
Third, because one understands the object of grasping, there arise the signs of attachment to the body and the signs of the conceit of "I am";
these are correctly eliminated through internal emptiness and the emptiness of non-apprehension.
Fourth, because of the thorough knowledge of the object to be grasped, there arises the mark of attachment to wealth;
this is correctly eliminated by means of external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

Fifth, because of the thorough knowledge of the objects of enjoyment—the correspondence between men and women, service, and requisites—there arise the mark of internal bliss and the mark of external purity and excellence; [these are respectively eliminated by internal emptiness and external emptiness].
This is correctly eliminated by means of internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) and essential emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Sixth, because one understands the meaning of establishment, there are immeasurable marks;
these are correctly eliminated by means of great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).
Seventh, because of the thorough knowledge of formlessness, there is the characteristic of internal tranquility and liberation;
this is correctly eliminated by means of the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

Eighth, because of the thorough knowledge of the meaning of the suchness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*), there are the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), the characteristic of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), and the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
These are correctly eliminated by means of the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth.
Ninth, because one understands the meaning of the purified *tathatā*, there are the characteristics of the unconditioned and the characteristics of non-alteration;
these are correctly eliminated by means of the emptiness of the unconditioned and the emptiness of non-alteration.
Tenth, because one attends to and contemplates emptiness as the very antidote to those aforementioned [signs], there arises the sign of emptiness;
this is correctly eliminated by the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
“World-Honored One!
When these ten kinds of signs are dispelled, what is it that is dispelled?
From what kind of sign does one attain liberation?”
“Good son! One eliminates the marks of the images that are the objects of samādhi;
one also eliminates that [state] from which liberation is attained—namely, the marks of the bonds of affliction.”
Good son! You should know that this is explained according to what is predominant: such emptiness treats such characteristics, yet it is not the case that each one does not treat all characteristics.
For example, ignorance is not incapable of producing all the various defiled phenomena up to and including old age and death.
"From the perspective of what is predominant, it is said that [ignorance] alone can produce formations (*saṃskāra*), because it is the immediate condition for these formations.
You should know that the principle here is likewise.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān, among these,
what is the general characteristic of emptiness?
If bodhisattvas understand this, how can they avoid failing in the characteristic of emptiness and remain free from overweening pride?”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Well-spoken, son of good family!"
It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a profound meaning, so that all bodhisattvas may not lose or destroy the characteristics of emptiness. Why is this?
"Good son! If bodhisattvas should fail or lose the characteristic of emptiness, they will thereby fail and lose the entire Mahāyāna.
Therefore, you should listen attentively, listen attentively!"
I shall now explain for you the general characteristic of emptiness. Noble son!

If, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), there is the absolute absence of all categories of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*)—whether defiled or purified—and if nothing at all is apprehended therein, this is called the general characteristic of emptiness in the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of superior samādhis are subsumed within this śamatha and vipaśyanā?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"Son of good family!
Regarding the immeasurable śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas that I have spoken of, and their immeasurable kinds of superior samādhis—you should know that all of these are subsumed within this."
“World-Honored One!
What are the causes of this śamatha and vipaśyanā? “Good son!”
“Pure ethical discipline and the right view established through pure hearing and reflection serve as its causes.
“World-Honored One,
what are the fruits of this śamatha and vipaśyanā?”
“Good son! Well-purified precepts, a purified mind, and well-purified wisdom constitute its fruit.
Furthermore, good son!”
One should know that all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas belonging to all śrāvakas, tathāgatas, and others, are the fruits obtained through this śamatha and vipaśyanā.
“World-Honored One!
What functions do this śamatha and vipaśyanā perform? “Good son!
Its function is to bring about liberation from the two types of bondage, namely, the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
“World-Honored One!
Among the five kinds of fetters spoken of by the Buddha, how many are obstacles to *śamatha*?”
"How many are obstacles to vipaśyanā?
How many are obstacles to both? "Good son!
Attachment to the body and wealth is an obstacle to śamatha;
being unable to follow one’s wishes regarding the various holy teachings is an obstacle to vipaśyanā;
delighting in living in company and being content with little—know that these are obstacles to both.
"Because of the first [reason], one is unable to engage in cultivation;
because of the second, the practice undertaken does not reach its ultimate consummation.
"World-Honored One!"
Among the five hindrances, how many are obstacles to śamatha?
How many are obstacles to vipaśyanā?
And how many are obstacles to both?
“Good son! Excitement and remorse are obstacles to śamatha;
lethargy, sleep, and doubt are obstacles to vipaśyanā.”
“Greed and hatred, you should know, both act as obstacles.
“World-Honored One!
To what extent is one said to have attained the complete purity of the path of *śamatha*?”
“Good son! When all forms of lethargy and drowsiness have been thoroughly and correctly eliminated, this is called attaining the complete purity of the path of śamatha.”
“World-Honored One!
To what extent is one said to have attained the perfect purity of the path of vipaśyanā? “Good son!”
"Up to the point where all restlessness and regret have been thoroughly and correctly eliminated—to this extent it is called attaining the perfect purity of the path of vipaśyanā.
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
"When various bodhisattvas bring śamatha and vipaśyanā to presence, how many kinds of mental distraction should they know? "Good son!
One should know that there are five kinds:

first, distraction of mental attention; second, external distraction of the mind; [third, internal distraction of the mind; fourth, distraction of the signs; and fifth, distraction of discursive thought].
Third, mental distraction; fourth, distraction regarding signs;
fifth, distraction regarding coarse heaviness.

"Good son! If bodhisattvas abandon the mental engagement associated with the Mahāyāna and fall into mental engagements associated with the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, you should know that this is called the distraction of mental engagement."

If one allows the mind to wander and disperse toward the five kinds of excellent sensual desires and their various distracting signs, among all discursive thoughts and secondary afflictions, and toward external objects of focus, know that this is called outward mental distraction.

If, due to lethargy and drowsiness, or due to mental depression, or due to relishing the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), or due to being defiled by any of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) associated with any meditative attainment, one should know that this is called internal distraction of the mind.

If one attends to and contemplates the various signs that are the objects of internal meditative concentration (*samādhi*) by relying on external signs, this is called "distraction of signs" (*nimitta-vikṣepa*).

If, taking internal mental attention as a condition, all sensations (*vedanā*) arise, and one conceives of a self through the body of coarse dysfunction (*dausthulya*) and gives rise to pride (*māna*), you should know that this is called "distraction of coarse dysfunction" (*dausthulya-vikṣepa*).
“World-Honored One!
As for this śamatha and vipaśyanā, from the first bodhisattva stage up to the stage of a Tathāgata, what obstacles do they counteract?”
“Good son! This śamatha and vipaśyanā, within the first stage (bhūmi), counteract the obstacles of afflictions, karma, and birth that pertain to the evil destinies.”
In the second bhūmi, one counteracts the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle transgressions.
In the third bhūmi, one counteracts the obstacle of desire and greed.
In the fourth bhūmi, one counteracts the obstacles of attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma.
In the fifth stage, one counteracts the obstacle of being unilaterally inclined toward either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
In the sixth stage, one counteracts the obstacle of the frequent manifestation of signs.
In the seventh stage, one counteracts the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle signs.
In the eighth stage, one counteracts the obstacles of exerting effort toward the signless and lacking mastery over signs.
In the ninth stage, one counteracts the obstacle of lacking mastery over skillful speech in all its aspects.
In the tenth stage, one counteracts the obstacle of not attaining the realization of the perfectly complete dharmakāya.
"Noble son! This śamatha and vipaśyanā, in the stage of a Tathāgata, serve as the antidote to the extremely subtle and most extremely subtle afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations."
Because one is able to permanently destroy such hindrances, one ultimately realizes the omniscient vision that is unattached and unimpeded.
Based upon the object of focus consisting of the fulfillment of what is to be done, the most supremely pure *dharmakāya* is established.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva, by diligently practicing in reliance upon *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
“Son of good family!

If bodhisattvas have already attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, they rely upon the seven kinds of true thusness (tathatā) and, regarding the dharmas as they have been heard and reflected upon, by means of a mind of supreme concentration, they engage in correct internal reflection upon the nature of true thusness that has been well-ascertained, well-contemplated, and well-established.”
Because he correctly contemplates suchness, his mind is even able to abandon the manifestation of all subtle marks, let alone coarse marks. Good son!

Regarding what is called "subtle characteristics," these refer to the characteristics apprehended by the mind; or the characteristic of experiencing; or the characteristic of discerning; or the characteristic of affliction and purification; or internal characteristics; or external characteristics; or internal-external characteristics; or the characteristic of thinking, "I shall practice for the benefit of all sentient beings"; or the characteristic of correct knowledge; or the characteristic of suchness; or the characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; or conditioned characteristics; or unconditioned characteristics; or permanent characteristics; or impermanent characteristics; or the characteristic of the mutability of suffering; or the characteristic of the immutability of suffering; or the characteristic of the difference among conditioned phenomena; or the characteristic of the similarity among conditioned phenomena; or the characteristic of perceiving that "having known all as all, there is all"; or the characteristic of the selflessness of persons; or the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena.
Regarding those active manifestations, the mind is able to relinquish them.
Because he dwells frequently in such practice, from time to time he thoroughly cultivates and purifies the mind from all fetters, hindrances, and distractions.

From this point onward, with respect to the sevenfold suchness, there arise seven distinct, individually realized, penetrating wisdoms within oneself; these are called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

By attaining these, one is said to have entered the Bodhisattva’s state of "correct nature free from birth" (*samyaktvaniyāma*), been born into the family of the Tathāgatas, attained the first stage (*bhūmi*), and is further able to enjoy the superior virtues of this stage.

Because he had previously attained śamatha and vipaśyanā, he had already acquired two kinds of objects of focus: namely, the object of focus that is a conceptual image and the object of focus that is a non-conceptual image.
Because he has now attained the path of seeing, he further realizes the object-condition that is the limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantālambana*).
Furthermore, as he progresses through all subsequent stages and cultivates the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he attends to and contemplates these three kinds of objects.
For example, it is like a person who uses a fine wedge to extract a coarse wedge.

In the same way, by relying on this skillful means of "using a wedge to extract a wedge," the bodhisattva eliminates internal signs; consequently, all signs concordant with the category of affliction are entirely dispelled.
Because signs are eliminated, the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) are also eliminated.
By permanently destroying all signs and heavy residues, one gradually refines the mind within each successive stage (*bhūmi*), according to the method of smelting gold.
"Up until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one further attains the object of focus for the fulfillment of what is to be done.
Son of good family!
It is because such a bodhisattva practices inner *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* correctly that they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one practice so as to bring forth the vast majesty and virtue of a bodhisattva?”
“Good son! If bodhisattvas skillfully understand the six bases, they are able to bring forth all the vast majesty and virtue of a bodhisattva:
first, skillfully understanding the arising of the mind;”
Second, skillfully knowing the abiding of the mind;
third, skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind;
fourth, skillfully knowing the increase of the mind;
Fifth, skillfully knowing the decrease of the mind;
sixth, skillfully knowing expedient means.
"What is meant by skillfully knowing the arising of the mind?"
It refers to knowing, as it truly is, the distinctions in the arising of the mind through sixteen modes; this is called skillfully knowing the arising of the mind.
Regarding the distinctions in the arising of the mind through sixteen modes:
first, there is the arising of the receptacle-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is stable and abiding yet imperceptible, namely the *ādānavijñāna*.

Second, the arising of consciousness with various modes of activity as its objects: this refers to the conceptualizing mental consciousness that simultaneously apprehends all objects such as forms, as well as the consciousness that simultaneously apprehends internal and external objects of sensation, or the conceptualizing mental consciousness that, in a single thought-moment, instant, or brief interval, enters into many meditative absorptions, perceives many Buddha-fields, and beholds many Tathāgatas.
Third, the arising of consciousness with minor characteristics as its objects: this refers to consciousness bound to the desire realm.
Fourth, the arising of consciousness with major characteristics as its objects: this refers to consciousness bound to the form realm.
Fifth, the arising of consciousness with an immeasurable aspect as its object, namely, consciousness associated with the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness;
sixth, the arising of consciousness with a subtle aspect as its object, namely, consciousness associated with the sphere of nothingness;
seventh, the arising of consciousness with a limit-aspect as its object, namely, consciousness associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Eighth, the arising of signless consciousness (*animitta-vijñāna*), which refers to supramundane consciousness and consciousness conditioned by cessation (*nirodha*);
ninth, the arising of consciousness accompanied by suffering (*duḥkha-sahagata-vijñāna*), which refers to the consciousness of the hells;
tenth, the arising of consciousness accompanied by mixed feelings (*vicitra-vedanā-sahagata-vijñāna*), which refers to the consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
11. Consciousness accompanied by joy arises; this refers to the consciousness of the first and second dhyānas.
12. Consciousness accompanied by bliss arises; this refers to the consciousness of the third dhyāna. 13.
Consciousness accompanied by neither-suffering-nor-bliss arises; this refers to the consciousness from the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
14. The arising of consciousness concomitant with defilement (*kliṣṭa*), namely, consciousness associated with the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
15. The arising of consciousness concomitant with the wholesome (*kuśala*), namely, consciousness associated with faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth;
16. The arising of consciousness concomitant with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely, consciousness that is not associated with either of those [two].
"What is meant by 'skillfully knowing the abiding of the mind'?
It means knowing the suchness of discernment (*tathatā-vijñapti*) as it truly is.
What is meant by 'skillfully knowing the emergence of the mind'?"
That is to say, knowing as it truly is the emergence from two kinds of bonds:
namely, the bond of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bond of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*).
One should skillfully know this and cause the mind to emerge from these.
“What is meant by ‘skillfully knowing the increase’?

It means knowing, as it truly is, that the mind which counteracts the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) increases when those [counteractive factors] increase, and accumulates when they accumulate; this is called skillfully knowing the increase.”
"What is meant by 'skillfully knowing the decrease'?

It means knowing, as it truly is, that when the mind—which is afflicted by the signs of its opposites and by coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*)—declines or diminishes, this [mind] also declines and this [mind] also diminishes; this is called skillfully knowing the decrease."
“What is meant by ‘skillfully knowing the expedient means’?

It refers to knowing, as they truly are, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), whether cultivating them or eliminating them.
Son of good family!...”
"In this way, a bodhisattva has already manifested, will manifest, or is currently manifesting the vast majestic power of all bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Blessed One has said:
"In the realm of nirvana without remainder, all sensations are extinguished without remainder.
Which sensations are extinguished therein?
“Good son! To speak in brief, there are two kinds of sensations that are extinguished forever without remainder. What are these two?
First, the experience of the heavy burden of the basis;
second, the experience of the objective realm which is its fruit.
It should be known that there are four kinds of the experience of the heavy burden of the basis:
First, sensation based on the form realm;
second, sensation based on the formless realm;
third, sensation of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) when the fruit has already been fully realized.
Fourth, there is the experience of heaviness (*dausthulya*) when the fruit has not yet reached fulfillment.
Regarding the experience when the fruit has already reached fulfillment, this refers to present experience.
Regarding the experience when the fruit has not yet reached fulfillment, this refers to the causal experience of the future.
The experience of the realm of those fruits also has four kinds:
first, the experience based on support; second, the experience of requisites; [third, the experience of the body; fourth, the experience of the environment].
Third, the feeling of enjoyment;
fourth, the feeling of attachment.

Within the realm of nirvana with remainder, although all feelings whose fruits have not yet been fully realized have already ceased, one experiences the feeling born of the contact of wisdom that serves as their antidote, experiencing it in common with others.
Alternatively, there is the experience of that fruit already fully accomplished.
Furthermore, two kinds of feeling have all been extinguished;
one now experiences only the feeling born of contact with clear [wisdom].
When one attains parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder, this [feeling] also ceases forever.
Therefore, it is said that within the realm of nirvana without remainder, all feelings cease forever without remainder.
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
saying: “Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!
You have now skillfully relied upon the perfectly complete and most utterly pure path of sublime yoga to question the Tathāgata.
Regarding yoga, you have already attained certainty and possess the highest proficiency.

I have already proclaimed for you the complete and most perfectly pure path of sublime yoga; all those who were perfectly awakened ones in the past and all those who will be perfectly awakened in the future have likewise taught it, and shall teach it in the same way.
“Sons of good family and daughters of good family, all should rely upon this courageous diligence and practice it correctly!
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“In the yoga of provisional designations regarding phenomena, If one acts with negligence, one loses the great purpose.”
Relying upon this Dharma and yoga, if one practices correctly, one attains great awakening.
To see something as obtainable and seek liberation from it, or to claim that such a view constitutes the attainment of the Dharma—
Maitreya, such a person is as far from yoga as the earth is from space.
One does not act for the sake of benefiting beings with a rigid mind; having awakened, one diligently cultivates the benefit of sentient beings.
When the wise perform this throughout the full measure of eons, they immediately attain the supreme joy free from defilement.
If a person preaches the Dharma out of desire, they are said to have abandoned desire only to take it up again;
though they have obtained the priceless jewel of the Dharma through their folly, they instead wander about begging for alms.
Regarding attachment to strife, clamor, and conceptual proliferation, you should abandon them and arouse supreme diligence;
for the sake of delivering all devas and the world, you should train yourself in this yoga!
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Within this Dharma-gate of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, by what name should this teaching be known?"
"How should I receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Good son!"
"This is called the teaching of the definitive meaning of Yoga; you should uphold this teaching of the definitive meaning of Yoga.
When this teaching of the definitive meaning of Yoga was spoken, within that great assembly, six hundred thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
three hundred thousand śrāvakas, free from dust and defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
One hundred and fifty thousand śrāvakas, having forever exhausted all outflows, attained liberation of mind;
seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the vast yoga of mental attention.
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Three;

Chapter Seven: The Perfection of the Grounds (4). Chapter Seven: The Perfection of the Grounds.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

As the Buddha has taught, there are the ten stages of a bodhisattva, namely: the Stage of Utmost Joy, the Stage of Purity, the Stage of Radiant Light, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage of Supreme Difficulty to Conquer, the Stage of Presence, the Stage of Far-Going, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Stage of the Dharma Cloud;
furthermore, he speaks of the Stage of the Buddha as the eleventh.
"In this way, how many kinds of purification are there in these stages?
By how many factors are they subsumed?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son! You should know that the various stages (*bhūmi*) are comprised of four kinds of purity and eleven divisions.
What are called the four kinds of purity that encompass the various stages?
That is to say: the purity of superior intention is subsumed under the first stage;
the purity of superior ethical discipline is subsumed under the second stage;
and the purity of superior mind is subsumed under the third stage.

Because the purification of higher wisdom becomes increasingly sublime in each successive stage, you should know that it encompasses [the stages] from the fourth bhūmi up to the Buddha-bhūmi. Noble son!
It should be understood that these four kinds of purity comprehensively encompass all the stages (*bhūmi*).
What are called the eleven factors that can encompass the stages? They are as follows:

first, because bodhisattvas, while on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), rely upon the ten dharma-practices and thoroughly cultivate the patience of resolute belief (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), they transcend that stage and enter the bodhisattva’s state of rightness and freedom from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).
By virtue of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas have fulfilled this portion;
yet, they are not yet able to act with clear comprehension when subtle transgressions manifest through inadvertence, and for this reason, they are still not fully perfected in this portion.

In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent application and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.

Yet, they have not yet attained worldly perfection, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), and the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining; for this reason, they are still not perfected in this particular aspect.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.

Yet, they have not yet been able to dwell frequently in the cultivation of those factors conducive to enlightenment as they have acquired them; nor has their mind been able to relinquish attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and attachment to the Dharma. For these reasons, they are still not perfected in this particular stage.

In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent application and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.

Yet, they have not yet been able to observe the principles of the truths as they truly are; nor have they been able to cultivate an attention that abandons the one-sided inclination toward either cyclic existence or nirvāṇa; nor have they been able to cultivate the factors of enlightenment subsumed under skillful means. For these reasons, they are still not perfected in this stage.

In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by means of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas achieve the perfection of this factor.

Yet, they have not yet been able to observe the流转 (saṃsāra) of birth and death as it truly is; furthermore, because they have developed a strong aversion toward it, they have not yet been able to dwell extensively in signless mental attention (animitta-manasikāra). For these reasons, they are still not perfected in this stage.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligence and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to perfection.

Yet, one has not yet been able to dwell in the cultivation of signless mental attention—uninterrupted, continuous, and extensive; for this reason, one is still not perfected in this particular factor.

In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas achieve the perfection of this factor.
Yet, being unable to relinquish effort within the state of signlessness and further being unable to attain mastery over signs, for these reasons, they remain incomplete in this respect.

In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by virtue of these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to perfection.

Yet, they have not attained great mastery over the teaching of the Dharma through its various names, manifold characteristics, distinctions in terminology, and all its categories; for this reason, they are still not perfected in this particular aspect.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas bring this factor to completion.
Yet, they have not yet attained the full realization and experience of the perfect Dharmakāya being manifest before them; for this reason, they are still not perfected in this aspect.
In order to bring this aspect to perfection, they practice with diligent effort and are thus able to realize it; by these causes and conditions, those bodhisattvas become perfected in this aspect.

Yet, they have not yet attained the sublime knowledge and sublime vision that are unattached and unimpeded throughout all objects of knowledge; for this reason, they are still not perfected in this respect.
In order to bring this factor to fulfillment, one practices with diligent effort and is thus able to realize it; by reason of this, this factor becomes fulfilled.
Because this factor is fulfilled, all factors attain fulfillment.
“Good son! You should know that these eleven kinds of divisions universally encompass all the stages.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is the first called the Stage of Supreme Joy?
And for what reason are they designated as the Stages up to the Buddha Stage?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!

Having accomplished the great purpose and attained the unprecedented supramundane mind, one gives rise to great joy; for this reason, it is called the first stage, the Stage of Supreme Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi)."
Because one is far removed from all subtle transgressions of the precepts, the second stage is named the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Because the samādhis and the dhāraṇī for retaining what has been heard attained therein serve as the basis for immeasurable light of wisdom, the third stage is named the Radiant Ground (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) attained therein burn away all afflictions, and wisdom is like a blazing flame, the fourth stage is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

Because one must practice those very same factors conducive to enlightenment with extreme difficulty through skillful means before attaining mastery, the fifth stage is named the Stage of Utmost Difficulty to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

Because one directly observes the flow and transformation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and because the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward signlessness (*animitta*) frequently manifests before one, the sixth stage is therefore named the "Manifest" (*Abhimukhī*) Stage.

Because one is able to enter far into the mental attention that is flawless, uninterrupted, and signless, which is contiguous with the stage of complete purity, the seventh stage is therefore called the "Far-Reaching" (Dūraṃgamā) stage.
Because one attains effortlessness through signlessness and is no longer moved by the active afflictions among all signs, the eighth stage is named the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi).
Because one attains mastery in teaching the Dharma in all its aspects and acquires faultless, vast wisdom, the ninth stage is named the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*).

Because the body of heavy impurities (*dausthulya*) is as vast as space, while the Dharma-body is perfected and pervades all like a great cloud, the tenth stage is named the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*Dharmameghā*).

Because one has eternally severed the most extremely subtle afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions, and having attained non-attachment and non-obstruction, manifests perfect enlightenment regarding all aspects of the objects of knowledge, the eleventh stage is called the Buddha Stage.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In these stages, how many types of delusion and how many types of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) exist as their respective antidotes?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son, within these stages there are twenty-two kinds of delusion and eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that serve as their respective antidotes.”
This means that on the first bhūmi there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of clinging to persons and phenomena; second, the delusion of the afflictions of the miserable realms;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the second bhūmi, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of subtle transgressions; second, the delusion regarding the various courses of karma;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the third stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of desire and greed; second, the delusion regarding the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining;
as well as their corresponding heavy residues (*dausthulya*) which are to be remedied.
In the fourth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*);
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) which serve as the objects to be remedied.
In the fifth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind toward the rejection and turning away from saṃsāra; second, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind toward the pursuit of nirvāṇa;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the sixth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of observing the forward flow of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they manifest; second, the delusion of the frequent manifestation of signs (*nimitta*);
and the corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are their respective counteragents.
In the seventh stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of the manifestation of subtle signs; second, the delusion regarding the skillful means of mental attention directed exclusively toward the signless;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the eighth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless; second, the delusion regarding mastery over signs;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) which serve as the objects to be remedied.
In the ninth stage, there are two types of delusion:

first, delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇīs of subsequent wisdom and eloquence concerning immeasurable teachings, immeasurable dharma-phrases, and letters; second, delusion regarding mastery over eloquence;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (dauṣṭhulya) which are to be remedied.
In the tenth stage, there are two types of delusion:
first, delusion regarding great supernormal powers; second, delusion regarding the realization of subtle secrets;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be remedied.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, there are two types of ignorance:
first, the ignorance of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge; second, the ignorance of extremely subtle obstruction;
as well as their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), which are the objects to be counteracted.
“Good son! It is by virtue of these twenty-two kinds of delusion and eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that the various stages (*bhūmi*) are established;
however, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is free from those fetters.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is most marvelous and rare; it brings about great benefit and great fruit, enabling all bodhisattvas to shatter such a vast net of ignorance and to transcend such a dense forest of heavy obscurations, thereby realizing Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi before their very eyes.”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many kinds of excellences are these stages established?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Good son,
there are briefly eight kinds:”
First, the purity of superior intention;
second, the purity of mind;
third, the purity of compassion.
Fourth, purity in reaching the other shore;
fifth, purity in seeing the Buddha, making offerings, and serving him;
sixth, purity in maturing sentient beings.
Seventh is purity of birth;
eighth is purity of majestic power. "Good son!

Regarding the purity of the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) and so forth, up to the purity of majestic power (*anubhāva*), within the first stage (*bhūmi*), as well as the purity of the superior intention and so forth, up to the purity of majestic power, in each subsequent stage up to the Buddha-stage—it should be known that these various purities become progressively more excellent; however, in the Buddha-stage alone, there is the purity of birth (*janman*).
Furthermore, all the merits possessed in the first stage are equally present in all the higher stages; however, one should know that the merits of each respective stage are superior [to those below].
The merits of all Bodhisattvas across the ten stages are "surpassable" (sopadhiśeṣa), whereas the merits of the Buddha-stage should be known as "unsurpassable" (anuttara).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do you say that the birth of a bodhisattva is the most supreme among all forms of birth?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Good son, it is due to four causes and conditions:
First, because it is produced through the accumulation of extremely pure roots of goodness;
second, because it is grasped by the power of intentional discernment;
third, because it compassionately delivers all sentient beings.
"Fourth, because one is personally unstained and is able to remove the stains of others.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason do you say that all bodhisattvas practice vast vows, sublime vows, and supreme vows?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!"
Due to four causes and conditions:
namely, that bodhisattvas are able to thoroughly understand the blissful dwelling of nirvana and are capable of swiftly realizing it;
yet they nevertheless renounce such swift realization and blissful dwelling.
Without conditions or dependencies, they give rise to the mind of great aspiration;
for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they dwell amidst manifold, diverse, and long-lasting great sufferings.
Therefore, I say that those bodhisattvas practice vast vows, sublime vows, and supreme vows.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of matters are there that these bodhisattvas should study?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Good son, the matters of training for a bodhisattva are briefly of six kinds:"
"Namely, the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Among these six matters that should be studied, how many are subsumed under the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*),
how many are subsumed under the training in higher mental cultivation (*adhicitta-śikṣā*),
and how many are subsumed under the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*)?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"Good son, you should know that the first three are subsumed solely within the training in higher ethical discipline."
Dhyāna alone is subsumed under the training in higher mind;
wisdom is subsumed under the training in higher wisdom;
I say that diligence pervades all of them.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Of these six matters that should be studied, how many are subsumed within the equipment of merit?”
"How many are comprised within the provisions for wisdom?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!"
If it is subsumed under the training in higher ethics, it is called being subsumed under the accumulation of merit;
