if it is subsumed under the training in higher wisdom, it is called being subsumed under the accumulation of wisdom;
I say that the two types—diligence and meditative concentration—pervade all of them.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these six matters of training, how should a bodhisattva practice and study them?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Son of good family,
one should practice and train in five kinds of applications:”
First, at the outset, one possesses intense faith and understanding toward the sublime teachings of the true Dharma associated with the *pāramitās* within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;
second, subsequently, one diligently practices the ten types of Dharma-activities through the sublime wisdoms consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
third, one maintains and protects the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
"Fourth, to draw near to true spiritual friends;
fifth, to cultivate wholesome qualities with uninterrupted diligence.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are these matters to be studied established as being exactly six in number?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son! There are two causes and conditions:
first, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings;”
Second, because they serve as antidotes to all afflictions (*kleśa*).
It should be understood that the first three [perfections] benefit sentient beings, while the latter three serve as antidotes to all afflictions.
Regarding how the first three benefit sentient beings: it means that through generosity (*dāna*), Bodhisattvas provide them with material requisites and thereby benefit them.
By means of ethical discipline, one refrains from harming, oppressing, or disturbing others, thereby benefiting sentient beings;
by means of patience, one is able to endure such harm, oppression, and disturbance, thereby benefiting sentient beings.

Regarding the latter three as antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*): it means that by means of diligence (*vīrya*), although bodhisattvas have not yet permanently subdued all afflictions nor permanently destroyed all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are nonetheless able to courageously cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*), such that those afflictions cannot deflect their application toward these wholesome qualities.
By means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they permanently subdue the afflictions;
and by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), they permanently destroy the latent tendencies.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason are the remaining pāramitās established as being only four in number?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"O son of good family!
It is because the preceding six perfections serve as its companions."

It means that bodhisattvas, by means of the articles of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), gather those sentient beings who have been included within the previous three perfections (*pāramitā*), establishing them in the categories of virtue; therefore, I say that the perfection of skillful means acts as an auxiliary companion to the previous three.

If bodhisattvas, due to the abundance of afflictions in this present life, lack the capacity for uninterrupted cultivation; and because of their feeble intention and inferior inclination, lack the capacity for abiding in the internal mind; and because they have not properly cultivated the conditions for hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, their meditative concentrations cannot give rise to supramundane wisdom.

He then gathers a small portion of inferior merit and provisions as a resource, forming a correct aspiration in his mind for the sake of having minor afflictions in future lives; this is called the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*).

Because of this aspiration, afflictions become thin and subtle, and one is able to cultivate diligence; therefore, I say that the perfection of aspiration acts as a companion to the perfection of diligence.

If bodhisattvas, by virtue of the causes and conditions of associating with virtuous friends, hearing the true Dharma, and applying correct mental attention, transform their inferior aspirations into superior aspirations and are also able to attain resolute conviction regarding the higher realms, this is called the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā).

By the power of this, one possesses the capability for the mind to abide within; therefore, I say that the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā) acts as an auxiliary companion to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā).

If bodhisattvas, through having already heard the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and having cultivated its objects well, are able to give rise to meditative concentration (dhyāna), this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

By means of this wisdom, one is capable of inducing supramundane insight; therefore, I say that the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā) acts as an auxiliary companion to the perfection of insight (prajñā-pāramitā).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what causes and conditions do you proclaim the six pāramitās in such a sequence?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"Good son, it is because it serves as the basis for the successive inductions."
That is to say, if bodhisattvas have no regard or parsimony for their bodies or wealth, they are able to receive and uphold the pure prohibitive precepts;
to protect these precepts, they practice patience;
having practiced patience, they are able to arouse diligence.
Having aroused diligence, one is able to accomplish meditative concentration;
having possessed meditative concentration, one is then able to attain supramundane wisdom.
For this reason, I have taught the perfections in this sequential order.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these six kinds of pāramitās, how many distinct categories and varieties does each one possess?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son,
each has three kinds."
There are three kinds of giving:
first, the gift of Dharma;
second, the gift of material wealth.
Third is the giving of fearlessness.
Regarding the three types of precepts:
first is the precept of relinquishing unwholesome conduct.
Second, the precept of generating wholesome conduct;
third, the precept of generating benefit for sentient beings.
Regarding the three types of patience:
First, the patience of enduring enmity and harm;
second, the patience of accepting suffering with composure;
third, the patience of discerning the Dharma through investigation.
There are three kinds of diligence:
first, the diligence of donning the armor;
second, the diligence of the application that gives rise to wholesome dharmas.
Third is the diligence of application for the benefit of sentient beings.
As for the three types of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
first, because it is non-conceptual, tranquil, utterly tranquil, and faultless, it is the meditative concentration of dwelling at ease, which counteracts the various sufferings of the afflictions.
Second, the meditative concentration that brings forth meritorious qualities;
third, the meditative concentration that brings forth benefit for sentient beings.
As for the three types of wisdom:
First, wisdom that takes conventional truth as its object;
second, wisdom that takes ultimate truth as its object;
third, wisdom that takes the benefit of sentient beings as its object.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason and by what causal conditions are the pāramitās called ‘pāramitās’?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son,
it is for five reasons:
First, because of being free from attachment;
second, because of being free from longing;
third, because of being free from fault.
Fourth, because it is non-conceptual;
fifth, because it is correctly dedicated.
"Being unstained by attachment" means not being stained by those factors that are contrary to the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Being without attachment" means that one's mind is not bound to the fruits, maturations, or requitals of any of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
"Being without fault" means that within these perfections, there is no intermingling with defiled phenomena, and one is free from practices that are not skillful means.
"Non-conceptualization" refers to not adhering to the intrinsic characteristics of these perfections as they are expressed by words.
"Correct dedication" refers to dedicating the perfections thus performed and accumulated toward the fruit of unsurpassed, great bodhi.
“World-Honored One!
What are called the factors that are contrary to the pāramitās? “Good son!
It should be known that this matter consists briefly of six types:
first, deeply perceiving the merits and advantages within the pleasures of wealth, sovereignty, and the various desires for joy and delight;
second, deeply perceiving the merits and advantages within the engagement of body, speech, and mind as they are freely exercised according to one's inclinations.
Third, regarding the inability to endure contempt from others, one deeply perceives its virtues and benefits;
fourth, regarding the failure to practice diligently due to attachment to sensual pleasures, one deeply perceives its virtues and benefits;
fifth, regarding dwelling in the clamor and worldly distractions, one deeply perceives its virtues and benefits.
"Sixth, one deeply perceives the merit and the advantages in seeing, hearing, perceiving, knowing, and in verbal conceptual proliferation.
"World-Honored One! [The Bodhisattva said.]
"What is the fruit and the maturation of all these perfections?
"Good son, you should know that there are also briefly six kinds:"
First, the attainment of great wealth;
second, rebirth in the happy realms;
and third, being free from enmity and destruction while possessing manifold joys and pleasures.
Fourth, he becomes a lord of sentient beings;
fifth, his body is free from affliction and harm;
sixth, he possesses a great and extensive lineage.
“World-Honored One!
What are called the defiled dharmas that are interspersed with the pāramitās? “Good son!”
It should be understood that, in brief, there are four types of application:
first, application lacking compassion;
second, application that is not in accordance with reason.
Third, because the application is not constant;
fourth, because the application is not earnest.
Improper application refers to when, while practicing one of the other pāramitās, one becomes distant from or loses the others.
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘non-expedient practice’? “Good son!

If, when Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the perfections (*pāramitā*), they are satisfied merely by providing material goods to benefit them, and do not cause them to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states, this is called "unskillful practice" (*anupāya-kauśalya*).
Why is this? Good son!
It is not merely by performing these acts toward sentient beings that one is said to provide true benefit.
For example, whether excrement and filth be much or little, there is ultimately no way to make them fragrant and pure.

Likewise, because sentient beings are characterized by the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), their very nature is suffering; there is no expedient means by which they can be made happy through the temporary benefit of material wealth alone. Only by establishing them within the sublime and virtuous Dharma can one be said to provide the supreme benefit.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of purity are there for all these pāramitās?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!
I never speak of the pāramitās as being anything other than the five aforementioned aspects of complete purity."
Nevertheless, based on these various matters both collectively and individually, I shall now explain the characteristics of the purity of the pāramitās.
Regarding the collective explanation of the characteristics of the purity of all pāramitās, one should know that there are seven kinds.
What are these seven?
First, a bodhisattva does not seek for others to know these dharmas;
second, having seen these dharmas, they do not give rise to attachment.
Third, one does not give rise to doubt regarding these dharmas, wondering whether or not they can lead to the attainment of great bodhi;
fourth, one never praises oneself or disparages others out of contempt;
fifth, one never becomes arrogant or heedless.
Sixth, one never becomes complacent and satisfied with having attained only a small measure;
seventh, one never, on account of these dharmas, gives rise to jealousy or stinginess toward others.
"To speak further of the sevenfold characteristics of the purification of all *pāramitās*, there are likewise seven types. What are these seven?
They are as follows: that bodhisattvas practice in accordance with the sevenfold characteristics of the purification of giving, as I have explained."
First, one practices pure giving through the purity of the gift;
second, one practices pure giving through the purity of ethical discipline;
third, one practices pure giving through the purity of view.
Fourth, they practice pure giving through the purity of mind;
fifth, they practice pure giving through the purity of speech;
sixth, they practice pure giving through the purity of wisdom.
Seventh, they practice pure giving through the purification of defilements.
These are called the seven characteristics of the purity of giving.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas are able to thoroughly understand all the training rules established for the code of discipline; they are able to thoroughly understand how to emerge from transgressions; and they possess constant ethical discipline, firm ethical discipline, ever-active ethical discipline, and ever-turning ethical discipline, training in all the training rules that exist. These are called the seven characteristics of the purity of ethical discipline.
"If Bodhisattvas develop deep reliance and faith in the ripening of the karmic results of their own actions, then when any harmful circumstance presents itself, they do not give rise to resentment;
nor do they respond with verbal abuse, anger, striking, intimidation, mockery, or by inflicting various forms of harm in return;
nor do they harbor feelings of enmity."
When being exhorted and instructed, one does not give rise to anger or distress;
nor does one wait for others to come and provide such exhortation and instruction;
nor does one practice patience out of fear or with a mind stained by attachment.
Not abandoning others simply because they have done one a favor—this is called the seventh characteristic of the purity of patience.
"If bodhisattvas penetrate the equality of diligence;
and do not exalt themselves or disparage others on account of their courageous and ardent exertion;"
Possessing great power;
possessing great diligence;
being capable and competent;
Firm and courageous;
never relinquishing the yoke regarding all wholesome dharmas—these are called the seven signs of the purity of diligence.
"If bodhisattvas possess the samādhi of meditative concentration that thoroughly penetrates the characteristics [of phenomena];"
There is the meditative concentration of the perfection of samādhi;
there is the meditative concentration of the shared samādhi;
there is the meditative concentration of the functioning samādhi.
There is the meditative concentration and dhyāna that is without basis;
there is the meditative concentration and dhyāna that is well-cultivated and refined;

and there is the meditative concentration and dhyāna cultivated through the immeasurable conditions of hearing the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. These are called the seven characteristics of the purity of dhyāna.
"If Bodhisattvas remain far removed from the two extremes of superimposition and denial and practice the Middle Way, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*);
by means of this wisdom, they understand according to reality the meaning of the gates of liberation—namely, the three gates of liberation:

emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—and they understand according to reality the meaning of intrinsic nature, namely the three natures: the thoroughly imagined, the dependent, and the perfected."

One correctly understands the meaning of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), namely the three types of absence of intrinsic nature: that of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), that of arising (*utpatti*), and that of the ultimate (*paramārtha*);
one correctly understands the meaning of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), namely within the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*);
and one correctly understands the meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), namely within the seven suchnesses (*saptatathatā*).

Furthermore, because it abides extensively in a single principle that is non-conceptual and free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), because it takes immeasurable composite phenomena as its object, and because it consists of *vipaśyanā*;
it is able to effectively accomplish the practice of "conformity to the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*). These are called the seven characteristics of the purification of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are the respective functions of these five signs?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:

"Good son, you should know that those signs have five kinds of activities. Namely, because bodhisattvas are free from attachment, they constantly and earnestly apply themselves with diligent practice toward the perfections (pāramitās) they cultivate within this present life, remaining ever vigilant and without negligence."
Because they are free from attachment, they embrace the causes for future heedfulness.
Because they are without fault, they are able to correctly cultivate the pāramitās that are perfectly complete, perfectly pure, and perfectly bright.
Because it is non-conceptual, the perfection of skillful means is swiftly brought to fulfillment.

Because of correct dedication, the perfections in all places of birth, as well as their desirable fruits and maturations, shall remain inexhaustible until the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Among these perfections (pāramitās) thus described, which is the most vast?"
What is undefiled? What is most luminous and flourishing? What is immovable?
"What is most pure?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!"
The nature of non-attachment, the nature of non-longing, and the nature of correct dedication are most vast.
They are faultless, non-conceptual, and free from defilement.
The discernment of what is to be done is most brilliant and flourishing.
Those who have entered the stage of the dharma of non-retrogression are called "immovable.
Those who are subsumed within the ten stages or the Buddha stage are called "most pure."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions do the delightful fruits and various maturations obtained by a bodhisattva through the pāramitās never come to an end?"
“Are the pāramitās also inexhaustible?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Good son!
"Because they arise in mutual dependence upon one another and are cultivated without interruption.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason do these bodhisattvas have deep faith and delight in the pāramitās, rather than in the various desirable fruits and karmic maturations obtained from such pāramitās?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Good son, it is due to five causes and conditions:
First, because the pāramitās are the cause of the most supreme joy and happiness;
second, because the pāramitās are the cause for the ultimate benefit of oneself and others;
third, because the pāramitās are the cause for the ripening of those desirable fruits in future lives.
Fourth, because the pāramitās are not the basis for any defilements;
fifth, because the pāramitās are not phenomena that are ultimately subject to transformation and decay.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For each of the pāramitās, how many kinds of most excellent majestic power are there?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son,
you should know that each and every pāramitā possesses four kinds of most excellent majesty and power."

First, when correctly practicing these perfections, one is able to abandon their opposites: stinginess, transgression of ethical discipline, mental agitation, laziness, distraction, and dogmatic views;
second, when correctly practicing these, they serve as the true provisions for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
third, when correctly practicing these, one is able to personally gather and benefit sentient beings within this very life.
"Fourth, when practicing correctly in this way, one will be able to obtain vast, inexhaustible, and desirable fruits of karmic maturation in future lives.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding all these perfections (pāramitās), what is their cause?
What is their fruit?
And what is their benefit?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"O son of good family!
All these pāramitās have great compassion as their cause."
The subtle, exquisite, and desirable maturation of various fruits has as its result the benefit of all sentient beings;
the fulfillment of unsurpassed, vast, and great enlightenment constitutes its great purpose and benefit.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all bodhisattvas are fully endowed with inexhaustible wealth and treasures and have accomplished great compassion, for what reason are there still sentient beings in the world who can be found in poverty?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son! This is due to the fault of the individual karma of these sentient beings!”

If it were not so, then since Bodhisattvas always maintain a mind intent on benefiting others and are constantly endowed with inexhaustible wealth and treasures, how could there be any poverty in the world, provided that sentient beings did not have their own evil karma to act as an obstacle?
For example, when hungry ghosts are oppressed by great heat and thirst, they see the waters of the great ocean as completely dried up;
it is not the fault of the great ocean, but rather the fault of the hungry ghosts' own karma.

In this way, the wealth and treasures bestowed by a bodhisattva are like the great ocean, free from any fault; it is merely that these sentient beings, through the power of their own karma, find no fruit, just as hungry ghosts, by the force of their own evil karma, find nothing to eat.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By means of which pāramitā does a bodhisattva grasp the nature of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"Good son, by means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one can apprehend the nature of all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature."
“World-Honored One!
If the perfection of wisdom can grasp the nature of all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature, why does it not grasp the nature of having intrinsic nature?”
“Good son! I never say that one apprehends the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature by means of the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Rather, the nature of the absence of intrinsic nature is free from all words and letters; it is realized within oneself.”
It is impossible to proclaim [the Dharma] while abandoning words and letters;
therefore, I say that the *prajñāpāramitā* can apprehend the nature of all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha has taught as the pāramitās, the near-pāramitās, and the great pāramitās.”
What is a pāramitā? What is a near-pāramitā? What is a great pāramitā?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:

"Good son, if bodhisattvas practice giving and other perfections for immeasurable time and thereby accomplish wholesome dharmas, yet their afflictions still manifest and they have not yet been able to subdue them—remaining instead subdued by them—this refers to the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) when weak or middling levels of aspiration are active; this is called 'pāramitā'."

Furthermore, by practicing generosity and the other perfections for immeasurable periods, they gradually increase and bring wholesome dharmas to fulfillment; yet the afflictions still manifest, though one is able to subdue them rather than being subdued by them—referring to those from the first bhūmi upward—this is called "near pāramitā."

Furthermore, by practicing generosity and other perfections for immeasurable periods, they become increasingly superior and bring wholesome dharmas to fulfillment; such that no afflictions manifest at all—referring to the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward—this is called the Great Pāramitā.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within these various stages (bhūmis), how many kinds of afflictive latent tendencies (kleśānuśaya) can there be?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son,
briefly there are three kinds."
First is the latent tendency that harms its companions, which occurs in the first five stages.
Why is this? Good son!

First, the "afflictions that destroy their companions" (*sahāya-ghātaka-anuśaya*): these refer to the non-simultaneously-arisen active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) which serve as the companions for the active simultaneously-arisen afflictions;

since those [non-simultaneous ones] will never again exist at that time, they are called "afflictions that destroy their companions. Second, the "feeble afflictions" (*durbala-anuśaya*): this refers to their subtle activity during the sixth and seventh stages, wherein they do not manifest because they have been suppressed through cultivation.

Third, the "subtle afflictions" (*sūkṣma-anuśaya*): this refers to the eighth stage and above; from this point onward, no afflictions manifest at all, as one relies solely upon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By the abandonment of how many kinds of *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness) are these various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) revealed?"
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"Good son, it is solely by means of two kinds [of causes]."

This means that by the abandonment of the heaviness (*dausthulya*) residing in the skin, the first two [stages] are revealed; furthermore, by the abandonment of the heaviness residing in the flesh, the third is revealed.
If the heaviness residing in the bone is abandoned, I say that one is forever free from all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), abiding in the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Through how many incalculable kalpas can such coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) be severed?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Good son!

It is after three great incalculable kalpas, or even immeasurable kalpas—because the measure of kalpas such as years, months, half-months, days and nights, one hour, half an hour, a moment, a flash, and an instant cannot be numbered—that [this is attained]."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the afflictions that arise within the various stages (bhūmis) of these bodhisattvas, what should their characteristics be known to be?”
"What are its faults?
What are its virtues?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
“Good son! There is no characteristic of defilement. Why is this?

These bodhisattvas, within the first stage, have definitively and thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of all phenomena. For this reason, it should be understood that when a bodhisattva gives rise to afflictions, they do so with full awareness rather than through ignorance; therefore, this is called the characteristic of being undefiled.
Since they do not produce suffering within their own bodies, there is no fault.
When Bodhisattvas give rise to such afflictions, they are able to sever the causes of suffering within the realm of sentient beings; therefore, they possess immeasurable merit.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!

Unsurpassed enlightenment possesses such great merit and benefit that it causes even the afflictions arising in bodhisattvas to surpass the roots of virtue of all sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas; how much more so, then, its other immeasurable merits?
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:"
"If there be the Śrāvaka-yāna or again the Mahāyāna, they are in fact but a single vehicle (ekayāna).
What is the underlying intention (saṃdhi) of this?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:

“Good son! Just as I have taught the various intrinsic natures of phenomena within the Śrāvaka vehicle—namely, the five aggregates, the six internal bases, the six external bases, and other such categories—in the Mahāyāna, I teach that those very same phenomena are of one single dharma-realm and one single principle; therefore, I do not speak of any differentiation among vehicles.”
Among them, some give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the meaning according to the literal expression; one class superimposes [existence] while another class negates [it].
Furthermore, regarding the principles of the distinctions between the various vehicles, they claim they are mutually contradictory, thus successively giving rise to disputes and arguments.
"This is what is meant here by the underlying intention (*saṃdhi*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The stages (*bhūmi*), the inclusion of mental images, the objects to be countered, The excellence of birth, vows, and the various trainings."
Because the Buddha taught this Mahāyāna based upon it, one who practices it well shall achieve great awakening.
He proclaimed the various natures of all phenomena, yet further declared that they all share a single principle;
whether in the Hīnayāna or the Mahāyāna, therefore I say there is no difference in the nature of the vehicles.
As it is said: "One falsely discriminates regarding the meaning of words, either by way of superimposition or by way of denial;
these two being mutually contradictory, the intellects of the ignorant fall into conflict."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within this Dharma-gate of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, what is the name of this teaching?”
"How should I receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: "Good son!"
This is called the definitive teaching on the pāramitās of the various stages; you should uphold this definitive teaching on the pāramitās of the various stages!

When this teaching on the definitive meaning of the perfections of these stages was spoken, seventy-five thousand bodhisattvas within the great assembly all attained the bodhisattva samādhi called "The Radiance of the Mahāyāna."
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eight: The Tathāgata’s Accomplishment of Purposeful Deeds (5).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“As the Buddha has spoken of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, what are the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!

If one skillfully cultivates renunciation regarding the perfections (pāramitās) of the various stages (bhūmis), such that the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is perfected, this is called the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
One should know that this characteristic is inconceivable for two reasons:
because it is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and because it is without purposeful activity (nirīha).
"Yet all sentient beings are attached to conceptual proliferation because they have something for which to strive.
"World-Honored One!
Is the transformation of the basis attained by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas called the Dharma-body?"
“Good son, it is not called the Dharma-body.
“World-Honored One!”
"What should this body be called?
"Good son, it is called the Body of Liberation."
By virtue of the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*), it is said that all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas are equal and identical;
by virtue of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is said that there are distinctions.
"Because there are distinctions within the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, its immeasurable merits possess the most supreme distinctions, which cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should I understand the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s manifestation?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son!..."
The activities of the transformation bodies of all Tathāgatas are like the arising of all varieties within a world-system;
they are characterized by being sustained and maintained, adorned by the multitude of the Tathāgata’s merits.
"You should know that while the characteristics of the nirmāṇakāya have arising, the characteristics of the dharmakāya have no arising.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should one understand the skillful means of manifesting the nirmāṇakāya?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Good son!"

Throughout all the Buddha-fields of the trichiliocosm, whether in royal families esteemed as preeminent by the masses or in great fields of merit esteemed by the masses, he simultaneously manifests the stages of entering the womb, birth, growth, enjoyment of sensual pleasures, renunciation, the display of ascetic practices, and the attainment of perfect enlightenment after abandoning those ascetic practices, manifesting them in successive order.
"This is called the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting transformation bodies.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How many kinds of distinctions in speech and sound are sustained by the bodies of all Tathāgatas,

such that through these sounds, sentient beings who are to be converted— those not yet matured— are brought to maturity, and those already matured take this as their object and swiftly attain liberation?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, the vocal sounds of the Tathāgata are, in brief, of three kinds:
First, the sūtras; second, the vinaya; third, the mātṛkās.
“World-Honored One!
What is the Sūtra? What is the Vinaya?”
"What is the *mātṛkā*? Mañjuśrī,
in whatever instance I reveal the various dharmas by relying on the summary topics (*saṃgrahavastu*), that is called a *sūtra*."
This refers to relying on four matters, or nine matters, or again, twenty-nine matters.
What are the four matters?
First, the matter of hearing and learning;
Second is the matter of taking refuge;
third is the matter of training and study;
fourth is the matter of awakening.
"What are the nine things?
First, the thing consisting of the designation of sentient beings;
second, the thing consisting of their objects of enjoyment;"
Third, the matter of their origination;
fourth, the matter of their abiding once originated;
fifth, the matter of their defilement and purification.
Sixth, the matter of their differentiation;
seventh, the matter of that which can be proclaimed;
eighth, the matter of that which is proclaimed.
Ninth, the matters concerning the various assemblies.

What are called the twenty-nine matters? They are those that pertain to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*): [as follows:]... [The list continues. ...These are the matters pertaining to the category of affliction.

Regarding the subsumption of all activities and the successive engagement therein: having formed the conception of a person (*pudgala*) within this very context, one forms such a conception regarding the causes for wandering in future existence—that is, regarding the causes for wandering in future existence.

The factors belonging to the category of purification consist of: the matter of binding mindfulness to the object; therein, the matter of diligent application of energy; the matter of the mind’s abiding in composure; the matter of dwelling in happiness in the present life; the matter of the skillful means for transcending all conditions of suffering; and the matter of that thorough knowledge.
This, moreover, is threefold:

because it is the basis for the thorough knowledge of perversion; because it is the basis for the thorough knowledge of misconduct toward external sentient beings based on the notion of "sentient being"; and because it is the basis for the thorough knowledge of internal freedom from overweening pride.
The basis for cultivation; the matter of realization; the matter of practice; the matter of making that firm; the matter of its modes of activity (*ākāra*);
the matter of its objects (*ālambana*); skill in observing what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned;
the matter of distraction; the matter of non-distraction; the basis for non-distraction; and non-abandonment of cultivation.
The practice of diligent application to activities, the practice of cultivating excellence, the practice of steadfastness,
the practice of embracing the noble conduct, the practice of embracing the retinue of noble conduct, the practice of penetrating reality, and the practice of realizing nirvāṇa— through these,
within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, one’s mundane right view transcends all non-Buddhist paths.
Regarding the attainment of the summit of right view and the subsequent failure to cultivate it—
due to a lack of cultivation within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya— it is called "retrogression. This is not because of a fault in one's views,
but is thus termed retrogression.
“Mañjuśrī! Wherever, based upon the śrāvakas and the bodhisattvas, I reveal the Prātimokṣa and the dharmas associated with the Prātimokṣa, that is called ‘Vinaya’ (Discipline).”
“World-Honored One!
By how many characteristics is the prātimokṣa of a bodhisattva subsumed? “Good son!
One should know that there are seven characteristics:
first, the proclamation of the rules for undertaking [the precepts];
second, the proclamation of the matters that constitute a defeat (*pārājika*).
Third, the proclamation of matters that accord with transgressions;
fourth, the proclamation of the intrinsic nature of having committed a transgression;
fifth, the proclamation of the intrinsic nature of not having committed a transgression.
Sixth, because it proclaims the confession of transgressions;
seventh, because it proclaims the relinquishing of the vows. "Mañjuśrī!..."
If, in this context, I definitively discern and reveal all phenomena through eleven modes of characteristics, these are called the *mātṛkā*.
What are the names of these eleven modes of characteristics?
First, the characteristic of the conventional;
second, the characteristic of the ultimate meaning;
third, the characteristic of the object of focus for the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Fourth, the characteristic of practice;
fifth, the characteristic of intrinsic nature;
sixth, the characteristic of its fruit.
Seventh, the characteristic of the reception of the instruction;
eighth, the characteristic of obstructive phenomena;
ninth, the characteristic of conforming phenomena.
Tenth, the characteristic of its disadvantages;
eleventh, the characteristic of its benefits.
"The characteristic of the conventional should be known as threefold:
First, because it proclaims the *pudgala*;
second, because it proclaims the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
and third, because it proclaims the functional activities of all phenomena.
Regarding the characteristic of the ultimate truth, it should be understood as being taught through the exposition of the seven kinds of suchness.
Regarding the characteristic of the focal object of the factors conducive to enlightenment, it should be understood as being taught through the exposition of all knowable objects in every respect.
"Regarding the 'aspects' (ākāra), it should be understood as the teaching of the eightfold contemplation. What are the eightfold contemplations?
First, because they are true and real;"
Second, because of abiding securely;
third, because of faults;
fourth, because of virtues.
Fifth, by way of the underlying principle;
sixth, by way of the process of transmigration;
seventh, by way of the logical reasoning;
Eighth, because of the general and the specific.
"Ultimate reality" refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

"Establishment" refers to either establishing the person (*pudgala*), or establishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of phenomena, or establishing [the four modes of] categorical, analytical, counter-interrogative, and setting-aside answers, or establishing the implicit, the explicit, the prophetic, and the differentiated.
Regarding "faults," it means that I have proclaimed the various phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) through immeasurable gateways of distinct disadvantages.
Regarding "virtues," it means that I have proclaimed the various phenomena of purification (*vyavadāna*) through immeasurable gateways of distinct benefits.
"Regarding 'principle' (naya), it should be known that there are six kinds:
first, the principle of true meaning;
second, the principle of realization;"
Third, the principle of instruction;
fourth, the principle of avoiding the two extremes;
fifth, the principle of the inconceivable;
Sixth, the intentional meaning (*abhiprāya*) and the underlying principle (*naya*).
"Cyclic existence" refers to the three periods of time, the three characteristics of the conditioned, and the four types of conditions.
"Principle" should be understood as being of four kinds:
First, the principle of dependence;
second, the principle of function;
third, the principle of establishment through proof.
Fourth is the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*).

Regarding the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*): it refers to those causes and conditions that are able to produce all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and give rise to conventional designations; this is called the principle of dependence.

The principle of efficacy refers to those causes and conditions by which phenomena are obtained, or brought to completion, or, once arisen, perform their various functional activities; this is called the principle of efficacy.

The principle of proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*) refers to those causes or conditions that enable the meaning of what is established, what is explained, and what is indicated to be successfully proven, thereby bringing about correct awakening; this is called the principle of proof.
Furthermore, this principle is briefly of two kinds: first, pure; second, impure.
It is called pure by way of five aspects, and impure by way of seven aspects.
"In what way is it called pure by way of five aspects?"
First, the characteristic obtained through direct perception;
second, the characteristic obtained by relying on direct perception;
third, the characteristic induced by analogies from within its own class.
Fourth is the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*);
fifth is the characteristic of the well-purified teaching (*suviśuddha-āgama-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding "the characteristic obtained through direct perception," this refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent by nature, all conditioned phenomena are suffering by nature, and all phenomena (*dharma*) are selfless by nature; these are what are obtained through worldly direct cognition (*loka-pratyakṣa*).
Such categories as these are called the characteristics obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding "relying on the characteristics obtained through direct perception," this refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary in nature, that there is a future world, and that pure and impure karma does not perish.
Because that which depends upon it—the coarse nature of impermanence—is currently observable;

because the various distinctions among sentient beings are currently observable as depending on their various karmas; and because the pleasure or pain experienced by sentient beings is currently observable as being based upon pure or impure karma.
Based on these causes and conditions, that which is not currently perceived can be inferred.
Such categories as these are called "the characteristics derived from what is presently perceived.

Regarding "the characteristics induced by analogies from one's own class," this refers to taking as analogies the birth and death commonly understood by the world within the internal and external aggregates of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-rāśi*); taking as analogies the various characteristics of suffering such as birth commonly understood by the world; taking as analogies the characteristic of lack of autonomy commonly understood by the world; and furthermore, taking as analogies the decline and prosperity commonly understood by the world in the external sphere.
One should know that such categories as these are called the characteristics induced by analogies from their own class (*svajātīya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding the "perfectly established characteristic" (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the characteristic obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣopalabdha-lakṣaṇa*), or the characteristic obtained through analogies from its own class based upon the characteristic obtained through direct perception. When these are able to definitively establish what is to be proven, one should know that this is called the perfectly established characteristic.

"The characteristic of well-purified verbal instruction refers to that which is proclaimed by the Omniscient One; for example, the statement that 'Nirvana is ultimate tranquility. Such categories as these should be known as the characteristic of well-purified verbal instruction."
“Good son! Therefore, by means of these five characteristics, it is called the principle of well-observed purity; because it is pure, it should be cultivated.”
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the characteristics of omniscience, how many kinds should be known to exist?"
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son,
there are briefly five kinds:”
First, whenever the sound of "Omniscience" appears in the world, there is no place where it is not heard universally;
second, they achieve the thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
third, they are endowed with the ten powers and are able to sever all doubts and delusions of all sentient beings.
Fourth, being endowed with the four fearlessnesses, he proclaims the true Dharma; he cannot be overcome by any opposing arguments from others, yet he is able to crush all false doctrines.
Fifth, within his well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, the Noble Eightfold Path, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and so forth, are all manifest and attainable.

Because it is thus produced, because it possesses these characteristics, because it cuts through the web of doubt, because it cannot be subdued by others but can subdue others, and because the noble path and the fruits of the śramaṇa are directly attainable—these five aspects should be known as the characteristics of omniscience.
“Good son! This principle of establishment by proof is established through direct perception, through inference, and through authoritative scripture.
By means of five aspects, it is termed ‘purified.’”
"In what way is it called 'impure' by virtue of seven aspects?
First, the aspect of the obtainability of other similar things;
second, the aspect of the obtainability of other dissimilar things;"
Third, the characteristic of being obtainable as all things of the same class;
fourth, the characteristic of being obtainable as all things of different classes;
fifth, the characteristic obtained through analogies from different classes.
Sixth is the characteristic of not being the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*);
seventh is the characteristic of not being well-purified verbal instruction (*suviśuddha-āgama-lakṣaṇa*).

"If all phenomena have the nature of being cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this is called the characteristic of obtaining all things as being of the same class (*sarva-sajātīya-prāpya-lakṣaṇa*). If all phenomena possess distinct characteristics of appearance, nature, activity, and the causes and effects of dharmas, such that by following each one of these distinct characteristics they are determined to be mutually and individually different, this is called the characteristic of obtaining all things as being of different classes (*sarva-vijātīya-prāpya-lakṣaṇa*)."

"Good son! If, within these other similar characteristics that can be apprehended, as well as within the analogies, there were any dissimilar characteristics, then for this reason, because the thesis to be established would not be certain, it is called the non-perfectly established characteristic."

Furthermore, because there are characteristics of other dissimilar classes that can be found within this [definition], as well as all characteristics of similar classes within the illustrative examples, for these reasons, since it is not determinate regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), it is also called the "not fully established characteristic" (*aparinispanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it is not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it is not a well-examined principle of purity, and because it is impure, it should not be cultivated.

If a characteristic is introduced by an inappropriate analogy, or if it is a characteristic of an improperly purified scriptural teaching, one should know that its essential nature is entirely impure.

"The principle of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā-yukti) refers to that which is the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the realm of phenomena—whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear; this is called the principle of the nature of phenomena."
“Regarding ‘general and specific’: this means that after first stating a single dharma in general, the subsequent phrases provide detailed distinctions and ultimate clarification.

Regarding ‘the characteristic of intrinsic nature’: this refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)—such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—which possess activity and objects as I have described; these are called their characteristic of intrinsic nature.”

"As for the characteristic of its fruit: it refers to the abandonment of all afflictions, whether mundane or supramundane, as well as the mundane and supramundane qualities of fruition that are induced by such abandonment. This is called the characteristic of attaining its fruit."

"Regarding the characteristic of receiving and revealing [the teaching]: it refers to receiving it with the wisdom of liberation regarding that very [object], and extensively proclaiming and revealing it to others; this is called the characteristic of receiving and revealing."

"As for the characteristic of those obstructive factors: it refers to those defiled phenomena that are able to act as obstacles to the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment; this is called the characteristic of those obstructive factors."
"Regarding the characteristic of conformity (*anuloma-nimitta*): it refers to those factors that are frequently practiced; this is called the characteristic of conformity.

Regarding the characteristic of disadvantage (*ādīnava-nimitta*): one should know that it refers to all the faults inherent in those obstructive factors; this is called the characteristic of disadvantage."
“That which constitutes the aspect of its benefits should be understood as all the virtues inherent in those conforming dharmas; this is called the aspect of its benefits.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain for the sake of the bodhisattvas the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇīs of the sūtras, the vinaya, and the mātṛkās, which are distinct from those of the non-Buddhists. By means of these uncommon dhāraṇī meanings, may the bodhisattvas gain entry into the profound and secret intentions regarding all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, listen attentively now;
I shall briefly explain for you the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇī, so that all bodhisattvas may skillfully penetrate the intentional terminology spoken by me."

“O noble son! Whether they be defiled phenomena or purified phenomena, I declare that all are devoid of activity and entirely lack a *pudgala*, because in every respect they are free from purposeful action.”

Defiled phenomena do not become pure after first being defiled, nor do pure phenomena become defiled after first being pure. It is because ordinary worldlings, within this body of heavy burdens (*dausthulya*), cling to the self-nature and distinctions of phenomena and persons, and take these latent false views as a condition, that they conceive of "I" and "mine.

Due to these false views, they think: "I see," "I hear," "I smell," "I taste," "I touch," "I know," "I eat," "I act," "I am defiled," and "I am pure. In this manner, various types of erroneous applications proceed.

If one knows this as it truly is, one will be able to forever sever the body of coarse heaviness, attain the non-abiding of all afflictions, achieve supreme purity, become free from all conceptual proliferation, rely upon the unconditioned, and be without further effortful application.
“Good son! You should know that this is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"All phenomena of affliction and purification Are devoid of activity and a personal agent.
Since I have taught that they are free from purposeful action, Defilement and purification do not occur sequentially."
Based on the latent tendencies within this coarse and heavy body, one takes them as a condition to conceive of "I" and "mine";
from this, one falsely claims "the view of self" and so forth, thinking: "I eat," "I act," and "I am defiled or purified."
If one knows this as it truly is, one will be able to forever sever the coarse and heavy body,
attain the stainless purity free from conceptual proliferation, and abide in the unconditioned without effortful application.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one understand the characteristics of the arising of the minds of all Tathāgatas?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Good son! A Tathāgata is not manifested by the arising of mind, thought, or consciousness; however, the arising of mental factors through the application of effort (prayoga) in all Tathāgatas should be understood as being like a magical transformation (nirmāṇa)."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the dharmakāya of all Tathāgatas is far removed from all conditioned application (prayoga);”
“Since there is no preparatory application (*prayoga*), how can mental phenomena arise?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!”
Due to the power of the preparatory application of skillful means and wisdom previously cultivated, the arising of mind occurs.
Son of good family!

It is like one who has fallen into a state of mindless sleep; although no preparatory application is made toward awakening, one awakens again by the force of the preparatory application performed previously.

Furthermore, it is like one who is currently in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); they do not apply effort toward emerging from that attainment, yet they emerge from it by the force of the effort previously exerted.

Just as the mind arises again from sleep or the meditative attainment of cessation, so too, it should be understood that mental factors arise once more in a Tathāgata due to the power of his prior cultivation of the preparatory practices of skillful means and wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgata, should it be said that it possesses a mind or that it is without a mind?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Good son!
It is neither with mind, nor is it without mind.”
"Why is this? Because there is no mind that relies upon itself, but rather a mind that relies upon others.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the conduct of the Tathāgata and the realm of the Tathāgata—what is the difference between these two?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Good son! The conduct of the Tathāgata refers to all aspects of the inconceivable and immeasurable merits shared by all Tathāgatas, which adorn the pure Buddha-fields.
The realm of the Tathāgata refers to all aspects of the fivefold differentiation of realms. What are these five?
First, the realm of sentient beings;
Second, the world-realm;
third, the dharma-realm;
fourth, the realm of discipline.
"Fifth is the realm of skillful means for subduing.
These are called the two kinds of distinctions.
Manjusri Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding these three—the Tathāgata’s attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment, his turning of the wheel of the true Dharma, and his entry into great parinirvāṇa—what characteristics should they be known to possess?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, you should know that these three are all without dual characteristics."
That is to say: it is neither the attainment of perfect enlightenment nor the non-attainment of perfect enlightenment;
it is neither the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma nor the non-turning of the wheel of the true Dharma;
it is neither the entry into great parinirvāṇa nor the non-entry into great parinirvāṇa.
"Why is this? Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is ultimately pure, and the transformation-body of the Tathāgata is constantly manifested.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If sentient beings generate various merits merely by seeing, hearing, and serving the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), what causal conditions does the Tathāgata have with respect to them?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Good son, it is because the Tathāgata is the causal condition for their predominant objective support."
"Furthermore, that emanation body is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Since there is no such preparatory effort, by what causes and conditions does the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata emit the great light of wisdom for all sentient beings and manifest the images of countless transformation bodies?
“Is it not the case that the bodies of liberation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack such qualities?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: “Good son!...”

For example, just as the sun and moon disks emit great radiance through two kinds of crystal gems—those of water and fire—whereas other water and fire crystals do not, this is because they are sustained by sentient beings of great majesty and by the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is like a mani jewel that has been carved and adorned by a skilled artisan, from which the image of a seal impression emerges, whereas this does not occur from any other uncarved jewel.

Thus, by means of the skillful means and wisdom that take the immeasurable dharma-realm as their object, and through the thorough cultivation and polishing thereof, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is fully realized and perfected. From this, the great light of wisdom is emitted and various manifested forms and images appear; such things do not occur solely from that body of liberation.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:”

"Through the majestic power and sustaining grace of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings are enabled to be born within the desire realm into great and wealthy families such as those of the Kṣatriyas or Brāhmaṇas, where their human bodies, wealth, and treasures are entirely complete; or they may attain the perfection of body and wealth throughout the heavens of the desire realm, as well as the form and formless realms."
“World-Honored One!
What is the hidden intent behind this?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“Good son! Through the majestic power and sustaining presence of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas, whether it be a path or a practice, wherever they may be, they are able to cause sentient beings to obtain the perfection of both body and wealth; accordingly, they proclaim this path and this practice for those beings as is appropriate.”
If there are those who can correctly practice this path and these courses of conduct, in every place they obtain physical form and wealth that are without exception perfect and complete.

If there are sentient beings who oppose and disparage this path and its practice, and furthermore give rise to a mind of malice and anger toward me, after their lives have ended, in every place they obtain physical form and wealth that are without exception inferior.

Mañjuśrī! By this cause and condition, you should know that the majestic power and sustaining grace of the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas not only cause the perfection of bodies and resources, but the sustaining majesty of the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas also causes the inferiority of the bodies and resources of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among all impure lands, what things are easily obtained?”
What is difficult to obtain?
Among all the pure lands, what is easy to obtain?
What is difficult to obtain?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Good son! In all defiled lands, eight things are easy to obtain, while two things are difficult to obtain.”
What are the eight things that are easy to obtain?
First, non-Buddhists;
second, sentient beings who suffer.
Third, the distinctions in the rise and fall of one's lineage and family;
fourth, the performance of various evil deeds;
fifth, the violation of the precepts (śīla).
Sixth, those in the evil destinies;
seventh, those of the lower vehicles;
eighth, bodhisattvas with inferior intentions and applications.
What are the two things that are difficult to encounter?
First, the sphere of activity frequented by Bodhisattvas who practice with the superior resolve; second, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.
“Mañjuśrī! In all the pure lands, the opposite of what has been described above should be known: eight things are extremely difficult to find, while two things are easy to find.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within this Dharma-gate of the Profound Unraveling of the Secrets, what is the name of this teaching?
How should I uphold it?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"Good son! This is called the definitive teaching on the Tathāgata’s Accomplishment of Purposeful Action. You should uphold this definitive teaching on the Tathāgata’s Accomplishment of Purposeful Action."

When this definitive teaching on the Tathāgata’s Accomplishment of What Is To Be Done was spoken, seventy-five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the great assembly all attained the realization of the perfected dharmakāya.
The Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra, Scroll Five.
